Determine and initiate the intercept or return path where one is supported. Where it is not, the item completes its delivery and the return happens afterwards - a cancellation does not reach into a van, and pretending it does leaves an unexpected delivery nobody has recorded
Is an external dependency involved in the cancellation?
Verify the cancellation actually took effect at the external party rather than assuming it did. A cancellation accepted by our system and not by theirs still produces the thing we cancelled
Does the cancellation carry a financial consequence?
Refund request → eligibility → approve, reject or review
nodes.detail: a cancellation with a financial consequence

nodes.headline: cancelled; remaining obligation stopped, completed scope preserved
nodes.detail: the remaining obligation is explicitly zero for the cancelled scope and unchanged for whatever was delivered. A new request for the same thing is a new obligation

edges.label: Some was completed
edges.when: part of the obligation was satisfied before the cancellation took effect

edges.label: Nothing completed
edges.when: no scope was satisfied

edges.label: Already dispatched
edges.when: something is with a carrier or executor and may still arrive

edges.label: Nothing dispatched
edges.when: nothing left our hands

edges.label: External party involved
edges.when: a supplier, executor or provider has to act for the cancellation to be real

edges.label: Internal only
edges.when: nothing outside our systems needs to change

edges.label: Money is involved
edges.when: something was paid for scope that will not now be delivered, or a charge applies to the cancellation itself

edges.label: No financial consequence
edges.when: nothing was paid, or what was paid matches what was delivered
a cancellation with a financial consequence

distinctFrom.because: Stopping a delivery and returning money are different decisions with different authority. Coupling them either refunds what was delivered or delivers what was refunded, and this journey hands the financial question to the lifecycle that owns it.

guardrails: A cancellation requested is not a cancellation.
A cancellation for fraud, compliance or manual review suppresses recovery outreach entirely. The reason it was cancelled is the reason not to chase it.
Recovery is scoped to the specific obligation that was cancelled. A later unrelated purchase does not close it, and counting one as a recovery overstates what the intervention did.
Cancellation does not erase completed fulfillment history.
Resource release affects only unused allocation belonging to this obligation.
A financial refund is a separate lifecycle with its own decision.
governance.reusableRule: Fulfillment cancellation stops the remaining obligation while preserving and reconciling any work or side effects that already occurred.
governance.entityScope: the obligation, split into what is completed, what is in progress and what has not started
governance.entityNote: The three scopes are treated separately throughout. Collapsing them either discards delivered work or cancels nothing at all.

identity.title: Identity claim → evidence → verified, rejected or more evidence
identity.purpose: Establish confidence in one specific identity claim, bound to the evidence that established it.

requires: a specific identity claim that a process or policy requires to be verified, at a stated scope
insufficientAlone: someone stating their name, which is a claim rather than a request to verify it
an account holding an attribute nobody has checked

nodes.headline: Identity verification required

Create the verification instance bound to the exact claim - which attribute, at what assurance level, for what purpose - and record it as PENDING. A verification that is not bound to a claim verifies nothing in particular, and is read later as having verified everything
Is the required evidence already available?

Request the minimum evidence this claim requires, and record the state as EVIDENCE_REQUIRED. Evidence is scoped to the claim - collecting more than it needs creates a liability without creating confidence, and asking for a passport to confirm a phone number tells the person we do not know what we are checking
until the requested evidence is received
nodes.detail: timeout after the verification timeout for this claim

nodes.headline: EXPIRED; the claim was never verified
nodes.detail: a new verification instance may be opened for the same claim. Expired is not rejected - nobody assessed the claim and found against it

nodes.headline: Validate the evidence against this claim's acceptance rules, recording the state as UNDER_REVIEW while it runs
What did validation conclude?
Does the policy allow another evidence round?
Request the specific additional evidence that would settle it, naming what is missing rather than repeating the original request
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a claim that automated validation cannot settle

nodes.headline: Verification failure → reason → retry, remediate, review or exit
nodes.detail: verification failing against a claim

nodes.headline: Mark this exact claim VERIFIED, at the assurance the evidence supports and for the scope it covers, together with the evidence that established it. Verifying one attribute verifies nothing else - a verified address says nothing about a verified identity, and the binding is what stops the second being read out of the first
VERIFIED for this claim, at this scope and assurance
nodes.detail: a different claim is verified on its own evidence, and this one is re-verified when its own validity lapses

edges.label: Available
edges.when: evidence sufficient for this claim at this assurance is already held

edges.label: Not yet
edges.when: the claim cannot be assessed on what is held

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the requested evidence is received

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: an open verification is a process held up somewhere else, and leaving it pending indefinitely blocks that process without anyone deciding to

edges.label: Verified
edges.when: the evidence establishes the claim at the required assurance

edges.label: Rejected
edges.when: the evidence does not establish the claim, and the reason is known

edges.label: Inconclusive, more evidence would help
edges.when: the claim is neither established nor refuted and further evidence could settle it

edges.label: Needs human judgement
edges.when: the evidence requires a person to weigh it

edges.label: Round available
edges.when: the number of evidence requests for this claim is within the policy limit

edges.label: Limit reached
edges.when: the claim has been through as many rounds as policy allows
a claim that automated validation cannot settle
verification failing against a claim

distinctFrom.because: Verification asks whether a claim is true. Authentication asks whether whoever is present right now controls it. A verified claim from last year says nothing about who is at the keyboard.

guardrails: An identity supplied is not an identity verified.
Verifying one attribute does not verify unrelated attributes.
Evidence is scoped to the claim being verified. Asking for more than the claim needs creates liability without confidence.
Evidence rounds are bounded by policy rather than repeated until something is accepted.
governance.reusableRule: Verification establishes confidence in a specific identity claim using defined evidence; it does not create universal trust.
governance.entityScope: the individual identity claim - which attribute, at what assurance, for what purpose
governance.entityNote: Verification belongs to a claim, not to a person. Two claims about the same person are two verifications, and neither carries the other.

identity.title: Verification requirement → collect evidence → resume blocked process
identity.purpose: Hold a verification dependency as its own state, blocking only the process that needs it and releasing it only after everything else is rechecked.

requires: a named process that cannot proceed, and the specific verification it requires at a stated scope
insufficientAlone: a general wish for higher identity confidence with no process waiting on it

nodes.headline: Process requires verification

Record which process is blocked, which verification it needs at what scope and assurance, why, and any deadline. Naming the blocked process is what stops this becoming a standing request for identity documents
Does an existing valid verification already satisfy this requirement at this scope?

Reuse the existing verification and record that it was reused rather than re-requested. Asking someone to verify again what they verified last week for the same scope is the fastest way to make verification feel arbitrary rather than protective
Initiate the required verification. The verification itself runs as its own instance; this journey owns only the dependency and the resumption
until the verification succeeds, or the verification fails
nodes.detail: timeout after the deadline of the blocked process, or its SLA

nodes.headline: How did the verification end?
Verification failure → reason → retry, remediate, review or exit
nodes.detail: a verification failing while a process waits on it

nodes.headline: Do the blocked process's other requirements still hold?
verification satisfied; the blocked process is free to continue
nodes.detail: a further verification requirement is its own dependency with its own instance

nodes.headline: verification satisfied, process still blocked on something else
nodes.detail: verification succeeding does not guarantee the process will - the other requirement is resolved on its own terms, and pretending this unblocked everything is how a customer is told twice that they are done

nodes.headline: The verification did not complete in time - what does the blocked process do?
blocked process expired awaiting verification
nodes.detail: a new attempt at the process opens its own dependency

nodes.headline: Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: a verification dependency outliving the blocked process's deadline

nodes.headline: held, visibly, awaiting verification
nodes.detail: the verification arriving later resumes this. Held is recorded as held rather than left looking like an unnoticed stall

edges.label: Already satisfied
edges.when: a current verification covers the same claim at the required assurance

edges.label: Not satisfied
edges.when: no current verification covers it, or the existing one is at a lower assurance

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the verification succeeds, the verification fails

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: how long to wait belongs to what is blocked rather than to the verification - a blocked payment and a blocked profile update do not deserve the same patience

edges.label: Succeeded
edges.when: the claim was verified at the required scope

edges.label: Failed
edges.when: verification did not establish the claim
a verification failing while a process waits on it

edges.label: All still valid
edges.when: nothing else the process needs has lapsed while this ran

edges.label: Something else is now missing
edges.when: another requirement expired or changed during the verification

edges.label: Expire
edges.when: the process cannot wait and lapses

edges.label: Escalate
edges.when: the process matters enough that someone should own getting it moving

edges.label: Hold
edges.when: the process waits indefinitely by design, visibly held rather than failed
a verification dependency outliving the blocked process's deadline

distinctFrom.because: FBK-49 is missing data - a value we do not hold. This is missing confidence - we may hold the value and have not established that it is true. The routes to resolving them share nothing.

guardrails: A verification already valid for the required scope is reused rather than re-requested.
The dependency blocks only the process that requires it.
Verification succeeding does not guarantee the blocked process will succeed. Its other requirements are rechecked.
governance.reusableRule: Verification dependencies should block only the process that requires them and release it only after current requirements are revalidated.
governance.entityScope: the blocked process plus the verification requirement holding it
governance.entityNote: One instance per requirement per blocked process. The same verification can unblock two processes and is not requested twice for them.

identity.title: Document submitted → validate → accept, reject or replace
identity.purpose: Keep uploading a document and satisfying a requirement as separate facts, and keep an acceptance bound to the requirement it was assessed against.

requires: a document submitted against an identified requirement
insufficientAlone: a file uploaded, which is a transfer rather than a submission against anything

nodes.headline: Document submitted
Record the document as SUBMITTED against the specific requirement it is offered for. Uploaded is not validated, and nothing may treat the submission as satisfying the requirement while it sits here

Validate the properties this requirement actually cares about: the document type, whether it belongs to the person offering it, readability, completeness, validity dates, the required fields, and integrity or authenticity where the requirement demands them
What did validation find?

Record ACCEPTED for this specific requirement, with what was checked. Accepted here is not universally valid - the same document offered against a different requirement is assessed again on that requirement's rules
ACCEPTED for the stated requirement
nodes.detail: the same document offered against another requirement enters as a new submission, because acceptance travels with the requirement rather than with the file

nodes.headline: Record REJECTED with the reason. A rejection that does not say what was wrong produces the same submission again
REJECTED for this requirement, with a recorded reason
nodes.detail: a different document may be submitted; this one is not reassessed unchanged

nodes.headline: Record CORRECTION_REQUIRED, stating specifically what is wrong and what would fix it
until a replacement is submitted
nodes.detail: timeout after the requirement's deadline, or this document's own validity end

nodes.headline: correction window closed; the requirement remains unsatisfied
nodes.detail: a new submission opens its own instance with the full history attached

nodes.headline: Link the replacement to the original and keep the original submission and its validation result readable. A replaced document is superseded rather than deleted - what was offered and why it was not accepted is part of the record
Is another correction round allowed?
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: repeated corrections failing to satisfy a requirement

edges.label: Valid
edges.when: the document satisfies this requirement's acceptance rules

edges.label: Correctable
edges.when: something specific is wrong that a better submission would fix - unreadable, cropped, an expired copy of a current document

edges.label: Invalid
edges.when: the document cannot satisfy this requirement whatever is resubmitted

edges.label: on event
edges.when: a replacement is submitted

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a correction request with no end leaves the requirement permanently half-satisfied, and the process behind it permanently waiting

edges.label: Round available
edges.when: the number of attempts against this requirement is within the policy limit

edges.label: Limit reached
edges.when: repeated corrections have not produced an acceptable document
repeated corrections failing to satisfy a requirement

guardrails: Uploaded is not validated.
Accepted for one requirement is not universally valid.
The original submission and its validation history stay auditable after a replacement.
Correction rounds are bounded, and the limit routes to a person rather than to a rejection.
governance.reusableRule: A submitted document satisfies a requirement only after validation against that requirement's current acceptance rules.
governance.entityScope: the submitted document, the requirement it is offered against, and its owner
governance.entityNote: Acceptance is per requirement. The same document may satisfy one requirement and fail another with different acceptance rules, and both results are true at once.

identity.title: Verification failure → reason → retry, remediate, review or exit
identity.purpose: Route a failed verification by why it failed, and keep our own failures out of the customer's verification record.

requires: a verification attempt that did not establish its claim

nodes.headline: Verification attempt failed

Classify the failure as INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, MISMATCH, UNREADABLE, EXPIRED_EVIDENCE, TECHNICAL_FAILURE, POLICY_FAILURE, REVIEW_REQUIRED or UNKNOWN. The class decides the route, and it decides something else: recording our own outage as an identity rejection marks someone as having failed a check they never got to attempt
What kind of failure was it?
Does the retry budget for this claim have room?
Explain exactly what needs correcting and offer the bounded retry. A retry offered without an explanation produces the same attempt again, which spends the budget without improving anything
Is a safe retry available within the backoff budget?
Retry with backoff, recording nothing against the person's verification history. Our failure is not their rejection, and the distinction has to survive into whatever reads that history later
bounded retry available; the verification instance stays open
nodes.detail: the retry runs as part of the same verification instance, against the same budget - a new instance would reset the count, which is how a bounded retry becomes an unbounded one

nodes.headline: Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: a technical failure that is not clearing

nodes.headline: Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a failure requiring human judgement, or a budget reached

nodes.headline: verification not possible on this basis
nodes.detail: a different basis or a different claim is assessed on its own terms; what would have to change here is the policy rather than the evidence

edges.label: The person can correct it
edges.when: insufficient evidence, unreadable evidence, or evidence that has expired

edges.label: Ours, and transient
edges.when: a technical failure on our side or a provider's

edges.label: Needs a person
edges.when: a mismatch, an explicit review requirement, or a failure nobody could classify

edges.label: Terminal by policy
edges.when: policy forbids verifying this claim on this basis at all

edges.label: Room to retry
edges.when: attempts against this claim are within the policy limit for its security sensitivity

edges.label: Budget spent
edges.when: the limit is reached - and repeated failure is also what a genuine person struggling looks like

edges.label: Retry
edges.when: the failure is transient and the budget has room

edges.label: Persistent
edges.when: the technical failure is not clearing
a technical failure that is not clearing
a failure requiring human judgement, or a budget reached

guardrails: Retry limits are policy-defined and bounded, and the bound is tighter where the claim is security-sensitive.
A technical failure is never recorded as an identity rejection.
Repeated retries do not bypass security controls. Exhausting the budget routes to a person, not to an acceptance.
The failure reason is preserved, because the route out depends on it.
governance.reusableRule: Verification recovery should follow the reason verification failed rather than treating every failure as equivalent.
governance.entityScope: the verification instance that failed
governance.entityNote: The failure belongs to the attempt. A technical failure and a mismatch are different facts about different things, and only one of them is about the person.

identity.title: Authentication challenge → authenticate, step up or deny
identity.purpose: Establish that whoever is present controls the required identity, at the assurance the context demands.

requires: a context requiring the actor's control of an identity to be established

nodes.headline: Authentication required

Determine the assurance level this context requires. Assurance is a property of what is being done rather than of who is doing it - setting it per user produces an over-challenged ordinary session and an under-challenged sensitive one at the same time
Does the existing authentication already meet the required level?
already authenticated at the required level
nodes.detail: a context requiring higher assurance re-opens this. Being authenticated says who the actor is and nothing about what they may do

nodes.headline: Issue the challenge appropriate to the required assurance level
until authentication succeeds, or authentication fails
nodes.detail: timeout after the challenge window

nodes.headline: challenge unanswered; nothing authenticated and nothing recorded against the actor
nodes.detail: a new attempt issues a new challenge

nodes.headline: What was established?

Issue or update the authenticated session with an explicit assurance level and an explicit validity. Both are needed downstream: without the level nothing can require a step-up, and without the validity nothing can decide the session has aged out
authenticated, at a stated assurance and for a stated validity
nodes.detail: authorization for any particular action is decided separately, every time - a successful login proves control of an account and entitlement to nothing

nodes.headline: Step-up requirement → stronger authentication → resume or deny
nodes.detail: control established below the assurance the context requires

nodes.headline: Authentication failure pattern → security check → recover or restrict
nodes.detail: an authentication failure

edges.label: Sufficient
edges.when: a current session holds the required assurance and has not expired

edges.label: Not sufficient
edges.when: no session, an expired one, or one at a lower assurance than this context needs

edges.label: on event
edges.when: authentication succeeds, authentication fails

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: an unanswered challenge is not a failure to authenticate and is not recorded as one; the attempt simply ends

edges.label: Authenticated at the required level
edges.when: the challenge succeeded at the assurance this context needs

edges.label: Authenticated below the required level
edges.when: control was established, at a lower assurance than the context requires

edges.label: Failed
edges.when: the challenge was not satisfied
control established below the assurance the context requires
an authentication failure

distinctFrom.because: This establishes who is present. ACC-75 decides what they may do. A successful authentication is an input to that decision and never a substitute for it.

guardrails: Authentication is not authorization.
A successful login does not prove entitlement to any particular resource.
An authenticated session carries an explicit assurance level and an explicit validity.
An unanswered challenge is not recorded as a failed authentication.
governance.reusableRule: Authentication establishes that an actor currently controls the required identity/account at a defined assurance level.
governance.entityScope: the authentication session, bound to an actor and an account
governance.entityNote: An authenticated session carries an explicit validity. A session with no stated lifetime is one that nothing can decide has expired.

identity.title: Step-up requirement → stronger authentication → resume or deny
identity.purpose: Raise identity assurance for a sensitive action, then check the action is still authorised before it runs.

requires: a protected action whose required assurance exceeds what the current session holds - a sensitive account change, a high-risk transaction, a credential change, a privileged action, or an unusual security context

nodes.headline: Action requires higher assurance
Preserve the requested action's full context, so it can resume rather than be reconstructed by the person from memory
Initiate the stronger authentication or verification this action requires, scoped to it rather than to the session as a whole
until the step-up succeeds, or the step-up fails
nodes.detail: timeout after the step-up window

nodes.headline: Was the higher assurance established?
protected action remains blocked; assurance not established
nodes.detail: a fresh attempt at the action issues a fresh step-up. Nothing is queued to execute if assurance is established later

nodes.headline: Revalidate the requested action against current authorization before anything runs. Passing a challenge raises identity assurance and authorises nothing - the entitlement, the resource or the policy can all have moved while the challenge was in front of the person
Is the requested action still authorised?
Access request → authorization check → allow, deny or step up
nodes.detail: a step-up completed with the action still authorised

nodes.headline: assurance raised; the action is no longer authorised and does not run
nodes.detail: the raised assurance stands for its own window; the action is attempted again on its own terms and decided again

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the step-up succeeds, the step-up fails

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a step-up that is not completed leaves the action blocked, which is the safe outcome and needs no further decision

edges.label: Established
edges.when: the step-up succeeded

edges.label: Not established
edges.when: the step-up failed

edges.label: Still authorised
edges.when: the action's authorization conditions hold at the raised assurance

edges.label: No longer authorised
edges.when: something the action depended on changed during the challenge
a step-up completed with the action still authorised

guardrails: Step-up success does not automatically execute the stale action.
The requested action is revalidated after the challenge, not before it.
The step-up is scoped to an appropriate assurance window and to the action that required it.
governance.reusableRule: Step-up authentication raises identity assurance for a sensitive action without replacing the need to revalidate that action's authorization.
governance.entityScope: the actor, the specific protected action and the authentication context around it
governance.entityNote: The step-up is scoped to the action that required it. Raising assurance once does not open every sensitive action for the rest of the session.

identity.title: Authentication failure pattern → security check → recover or restrict
identity.purpose: Tell an ordinary forgotten password apart from an account under attack, without converting the first into the second.

requires: authentication failures crossing a meaningful threshold, or matching a pattern the detection considers notable
insufficientAlone: one failed password attempt, which is the most common event in this category
a single failure from an unfamiliar device

nodes.headline: Authentication failure pattern

Evaluate the context around the failures: how fast they arrived, from what device and context, whether a credential reset is in play, whether the shape matches a known attack, and whether any session succeeded. A model's score orders the work and concludes nothing - what it produces is a case to look at, not an attacker
What does the evidence actually support?
ordinary failure pattern; nothing security-specific applied
nodes.detail: the usual recovery routes remain open to them, unchanged. Treating this as an attack would lock out mostly legitimate people, which is the failure mode this branch exists to hold open

nodes.headline: Account recovery request → prove control → restore secure access
nodes.detail: a legitimate-looking actor with no way through normal authentication

nodes.headline: Apply the smallest restriction the evidence justifies, and record what justified it. Most signals in this category are false positives, and for those the restriction is the entire customer-visible incident
Suspected account compromise → contain → verify → recover or clear
nodes.detail: a failure pattern that ordinary error does not explain

edges.label: Ordinary user error
edges.when: the pattern looks like someone who has forgotten a password - human pacing, a familiar device, no other signal

edges.label: The person cannot get in and needs a route back
edges.when: repeated legitimate-looking failures with no way forward through normal authentication

edges.label: Material security risk
edges.when: velocity, context change or attack-shaped behaviour that ordinary error does not explain
a legitimate-looking actor with no way through normal authentication
a failure pattern that ordinary error does not explain

distinctFrom.because: This weighs whether failures mean anything. IDN-90 starts from a material compromise signal and contains first. The route between them exists, and it is deliberately a decision rather than a default.

guardrails: One failed password attempt is not a compromise.
A risk model's output is not a confirmed attacker. It orders investigation and concludes nothing.
Any security response uses the smallest necessary scope.
governance.reusableRule: Authentication failure patterns should trigger proportionate security evaluation rather than converting ordinary mistakes into confirmed compromise.
governance.entityScope: the account plus the authentication activity observed against it
governance.entityNote: The pattern belongs to the account. A shared IP producing failures across many accounts is a different signal, assessed at a different scope.

identity.title: Account recovery request → prove control → restore secure access
identity.purpose: Give someone a way back into an account they can no longer authenticate to, without that route being weaker than the one it replaces.

requires: a valid recovery request against an identified account

nodes.headline: Account recovery initiated
Determine the recovery basis available and read the account's current security state. What is happening on the account changes what recovery is allowed to do
Is there an active compromise or security incident on this account?
Suspected account compromise → contain → verify → recover or clear
nodes.detail: a recovery request arriving during an open security incident

nodes.headline: Collect only the evidence this recovery basis requires. Recovery is not an opportunity to gather more than normal authentication would, and it must not be an easier route to the same access than the one it replaces - it exists for the case where normal authentication has already failed, which makes it the door an attacker reaches for first
until proof of control or identity is provided, or the attempt fails
nodes.detail: timeout after the recovery window

nodes.headline: recovery window closed without sufficient proof
nodes.detail: a new recovery request opens its own case, with this one in the history

nodes.headline: Is the proof sufficient for the assurance this account requires?

Invalidate the credentials and sessions that are no longer safe, before establishing anything new. An old credential left active after a recovery is precisely the thing the recovery existed to remove, and the order matters - new access first would leave both live at once
Establish secure replacement access at the assurance this account requires
Verify the recovered state: that the intended access works, and that the invalidated credentials genuinely no longer do. The second half is the one that gets skipped
secure control of the existing account restored
nodes.detail: this recovered one account and merged nothing. Two identities that turn out to be one person is a different problem with different evidence

nodes.headline: With insufficient proof, what does policy allow?
further evidence may be provided within the recovery window
nodes.detail: the same case continues; the window is not restarted by another attempt

nodes.headline: Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: recovery evidence that needs a person to weigh it

nodes.headline: recovery denied; account access unchanged
nodes.detail: a new request with genuinely new evidence may be assessed; repeating the same evidence is not new evidence

edges.label: Incident open
edges.when: a compromise is suspected or confirmed and containment is in force

edges.label: No incident
edges.when: the account is simply unreachable by its owner
a recovery request arriving during an open security incident

edges.label: on event
edges.when: proof of control or identity is provided, the attempt fails

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: an open recovery case is a standing invitation to keep trying, and closing it is part of not being a weaker route

edges.label: Sufficient
edges.when: the requester has demonstrated control or entitlement at the required level

edges.label: Insufficient
edges.when: the evidence does not reach the required level

edges.label: Further evidence
edges.when: the recovery basis allows another route to proof within the window

edges.label: Manual review
edges.when: a person should weigh what has been offered

edges.label: Deny
edges.when: no route to sufficient proof remains
recovery evidence that needs a person to weigh it

distinctFrom.because: Verification establishes that a claim is true. Recovery establishes that this requester is entitled to regain control of a specific account, which a true claim about their identity does not by itself demonstrate.

guardrails: Recovery does not weaken normal security controls. It is a different route to the same assurance, not a lower one.
Unsafe credentials and sessions are invalidated before replacement access is established, not after.
Account recovery is not identity merge.
The recovery window is not restarted by repeated attempts.
governance.reusableRule: Account recovery restores secure control of an existing account only after sufficient evidence that the requester is entitled to regain control.
governance.entityScope: the account plus this recovery case
governance.entityNote: Recovery restores control of one existing account. It never merges identities, and it never creates a second account for the same person as a shortcut.

identity.title: Identity attribute change → verify if required → update → propagate
identity.purpose: Change an identity attribute safely, and reconcile everything that depended on the old value independently rather than by inheritance.

requires: a change to an identity attribute, requested by the holder or received from an authoritative source

nodes.headline: Identity attribute change

Determine the attribute's sensitivity and what verification the change requires. Changing a display name and changing a legal name are not the same operation, and neither is changing a recovery address
Does this change require additional verification?

Verify current control of the account and, where policy requires it, the new attribute itself. An attacker holding a live session must not be able to move the recovery address on the strength of that session alone
until the verification succeeds, or the verification fails
nodes.detail: timeout after the verification window for this change

nodes.headline: Was the required control established?
change not applied; the attribute stands as it was
nodes.detail: a new request is verified on its own terms. Nothing partial was written, so no downstream system holds a value that was never confirmed

nodes.headline: Is the change itself valid?
change rejected as invalid
nodes.detail: a corrected value may be submitted

nodes.headline: Update the authoritative identity record, preserving the previous value where policy permits, the new value, when it took effect, the source, and the verification evidence and status. Identity history is not silently overwritten where auditability is required - what someone was called, and when that changed, is often the whole question later
Propagate to dependent systems carrying origin and version, so a stale update arriving late cannot restore the previous value
Does this change affect credentials, contactability or permissions?

Re-evaluate each dependent independently. A new email address inherits neither the old one's deliverability nor its consent - the new address starts with its own contactability state and its own permission, both empty unless policy explicitly says otherwise. Credentials tied to the old value are assessed on their own terms, and so are permissions that rested on it
identity updated; each dependent re-evaluated on its own terms
nodes.detail: each dependent's own journey owns what happens next - contactability, permission and credential lifecycles are separately triggered, because they have different owners and different rules

nodes.headline: identity updated; nothing depended on the previous value
nodes.detail: a further change to the same attribute is assessed on its own sensitivity

edges.label: Verification required
edges.when: the attribute is sensitive, or is itself a route back into the account

edges.label: Not required
edges.when: the attribute carries no security or legal weight

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the verification succeeds, the verification fails

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: an unverified sensitive change is not applied by default, so an unanswered verification simply leaves the attribute as it was

edges.label: Verified
edges.when: control and, where required, the new attribute are established

edges.label: Not verified
edges.when: verification did not succeed

edges.label: Valid
edges.when: the new value is well-formed, permitted and not in conflict with another record

edges.label: Invalid
edges.when: the value cannot be accepted - malformed, prohibited, or already held elsewhere

edges.label: Dependents affected
edges.when: the attribute is used as a credential, as a contact point, or as the basis of a permission

edges.label: Nothing depends on it
edges.when: the attribute is descriptive only

guardrails: Changing an email does not transfer the old address's contactability or its consent to the new one.
Identity history is not silently overwritten where auditability is required.
A stale update never restores a previous value - propagation carries origin and version so a late arrival is discarded.
A sensitive change is not applied on the strength of an existing session alone.
governance.reusableRule: Identity attribute changes should update the authoritative identity while independently reconciling any permissions, credentials or contact points that depend on that attribute.
governance.entityScope: the person or account plus the specific attribute changing
governance.entityNote: Each dependent - a credential, a contact point, a permission - is reconciled on its own terms. None of them travels with the attribute automatically.

identity.title: Suspected account compromise → contain → verify → recover or clear
identity.purpose: Limit the damage a possible compromise could do while the question is still open, and reach a conclusion that can go either way.

requires: a material signal: a credential-theft indication, an unauthorised sensitive change, a credible report from the owner, a high-confidence detection, or a suspicious session combined with a consequential action
insufficientAlone: a single failed login
a login from an unfamiliar location with no consequential action behind it

nodes.headline: Material compromise signal

Determine the affected scope - which sessions, which credentials, which sensitive capabilities. Scope is the whole question here, because most signals in this category turn out to be false positives, and for those the containment is the entire customer-visible incident
Is precautionary containment justified by the evidence?

Invalidate or restrict the affected sessions, credentials and sensitive capabilities, at the smallest scope the evidence justifies. Containment is reversible by design and does not erase forensic or audit history - the record of what happened is the only thing the investigation has to work with
Open the security recovery state without restricting anything, recording that containment was considered and judged unnecessary. Suspected is not confirmed, and the record says which one this is
until the owner is verified, or the security review concludes
nodes.detail: timeout after the resolution SLA for this incident class

nodes.headline: What did the investigation establish?

Revoke the affected credentials and sessions, and correct the unauthorised changes where correction is valid. Unauthorised financial or business actions are not corrected here - each carries its own dispute or correction lifecycle with its own evidence rules and its own authority, and reversing them from a security incident would bypass both
Capability restoration → revalidate → restore safely
nodes.detail: a confirmed compromise moving to secure restoration

nodes.headline: Record the signal as cleared, keeping it in the security history. A cleared suspicion is still a fact about what was seen, and erasing it makes a recurrence look like a first occurrence - which is the pattern most worth catching
Capability restoration → revalidate → restore safely
nodes.detail: a cleared incident whose restrictions should be lifted

nodes.headline: The SLA passed without a conclusion - what now?
incident open; scoped restriction continues
nodes.detail: the investigation continues and reaches its conclusion on its own. Suspected remains suspected - it does not become confirmed by lasting longer

nodes.headline: Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: an incident the automated path could not resolve within its SLA

edges.label: Contain now
edges.when: what could happen while the question is open outweighs the cost of restricting someone who turns out to be legitimate

edges.label: Investigate without restricting
edges.when: the signal warrants investigation and nothing needs preventing in the meantime

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the owner is verified, the security review concludes

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: an open incident with containment in force is costing a possibly-innocent person their access every day it continues, so an undecided one escalates rather than settles

edges.label: Compromise confirmed
edges.when: the evidence establishes unauthorised access

edges.label: Cleared
edges.when: the owner is verified and the activity is explained
a confirmed compromise moving to secure restoration
a cleared incident whose restrictions should be lifted

edges.label: Continue scoped restriction
edges.when: the evidence still supports restricting at the current scope while work continues

edges.label: Manual review
edges.when: a person should decide, because the automated path has produced nothing
an incident the automated path could not resolve within its SLA

distinctFrom.because: Suspension restricts for a stated business reason and expects to be resolved by that reason going away. This restricts on incomplete evidence about an adversary, which is why it opens an investigation rather than a review.

guardrails: Suspected is not confirmed. The two are separate states and containment belongs to the first.
Containment does not erase forensic or audit history.
Restoration never blindly reactivates old credentials, sessions or permissions - it rebuilds from current valid state.
Unauthorised financial or business actions are corrected through their own dispute lifecycles, not from inside the incident.
Containment uses the smallest scope the evidence justifies, because most signals here are false positives.
governance.reusableRule: Suspected compromise requires reversible containment and evidence-based recovery before normal account control is restored.
governance.entityScope: the account plus this security incident and the scope it affects
governance.entityNote: The incident is its own record with its own history. Containment attaches to it, and both survive whichever way the investigation concludes.

identity.title: Correlated failure detection → incident candidate → confirm or reject
identity.purpose: Establish whether several failures actually share a cause, before treating them as one thing.

requires: multiple failures or anomalies across entities, exceeding a meaningful correlation threshold
insufficientAlone: a spike in alert volume, which is a count rather than a correlation
several failures happening at once, which is often several failures happening at once

nodes.headline: Correlated failures exceed incident threshold

Correlate by time, service or dependency, region, version, provider, resource cohort, failure signature and shared infrastructure. What is being tested is whether these failures plausibly share a cause, rather than whether there are a lot of them

Preserve the link from the candidate to each individual affected entity, and keep each entity's own case open. A correlation that absorbs its members leaves every affected customer without a case of their own, and when the incident closes they have nothing left to point at
What does the correlating evidence support?

Retain the individual cases as independent, and record why they were not merged. Several failures at once is often several failures at once - merging them for operational convenience gives each customer a generic status page instead of an answer to their specific problem
no incident; the individual cases continue independently
nodes.detail: further correlated evidence reopens the question. Not merging now does not prevent an incident being confirmed later on better evidence

nodes.headline: Record INCIDENT_CANDIDATE and investigate. Candidate is a real state - it starts a look without asserting a shared cause to anybody, and it is what stops a hunch from becoming a status-page announcement
until evidence establishes a shared cause, or evidence rules a shared cause out
nodes.detail: timeout after the candidate investigation window

nodes.headline: Record INCIDENT_CONFIRMED with the correlating evidence that supports it. What is asserted is a shared cause - not that it is known, but that these failures belong together
Incident confirmed → determine severity and blast radius → assign command
nodes.detail: an incident confirmed on correlating evidence

edges.label: A shared cause
edges.when: the failures share a dependency, cohort, signature or infrastructure in a way that explains them together

edges.label: Independent failures
edges.when: the correlation is coincidental and each failure has its own explanation

edges.label: Insufficient evidence
edges.when: a shared cause is plausible and unestablished

edges.label: on event
edges.when: evidence establishes a shared cause, evidence rules a shared cause out

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a candidate held open indefinitely is neither an incident anybody is responding to nor a set of cases anybody is working, and both populations wait
an incident confirmed on correlating evidence

distinctFrom.because: RSK-192 assesses risk evidence about one actor or transaction. This asks whether failures across many unrelated entities plausibly share an operational cause - a question about the system rather than about anybody using it.

guardrails: Multiple failures are not automatically one incident.
Unrelated customer cases are never merged for operational convenience.
Correlation preserves the linkage to each individual affected entity.
governance.reusableRule: An incident should be created only when evidence shows multiple failures plausibly share a common operational cause.
governance.entityScope: the incident candidate and every individual failure correlated into it
governance.entityNote: Each affected entity keeps its own case and its own link. The incident is a layer above them rather than a replacement for them.

identity.title: Incident confirmed → determine severity and blast radius → assign command
identity.purpose: Establish what is actually affected, how badly, and who is running the response.

requires: a confirmed incident with its correlating evidence and affected entities

nodes.headline: Incident confirmed
Determine the affected systems, capabilities, regions, customers and accounts, dependencies, the start time, the current impact and the business criticality

Set the severity from the actual operational impact. A high event count is not a severity - a retry storm generates a hundred thousand events and affects nobody, and a single failing payment path generates twelve and affects everything downstream of it

Assign incident ownership and command according to the operating model, and record it separately from the owners of the individual cases. The incident owner runs the systemic response; the case owners still owe their customers an answer, and one absorbing the other means whichever survives stops doing the other job
Record ACTIVE_INCIDENT with the scope, the severity and the command as established
Has the affected scope grown since the incident was confirmed?

Expand the blast radius and re-derive the severity from it. A blast radius fixed at confirmation time understates every incident that spreads, which is most of them - and the response level set against the original scope is then wrong for the whole rest of the incident
What does the response need first?
Incident → contain and mitigate → preserve critical operations
nodes.detail: an active incident needing immediate impact reduction

nodes.headline: Root cause investigation → hypothesis → confirm or reject → corrective action
nodes.detail: an active incident where understanding comes before acting

nodes.headline: Record that the impact ended before the response engaged, preserving the incident and its evidence. A self-resolving incident is still an incident that happened, and it is usually the first occurrence of something that will recur
impact ended before response; the incident and its evidence are preserved
nodes.detail: recurrence is assessed against this record. An incident that resolved itself once and returns is a pattern rather than two coincidences

edges.label: It has
edges.when: a new cohort, region, dependency or capability is found affected

edges.label: It has not
edges.when: the blast radius as established still holds

edges.label: Immediate containment
edges.when: the impact is ongoing and reducing it does not have to wait for a cause

edges.label: Investigation first
edges.when: the impact is bounded or already stopped, and acting without understanding risks making it worse

edges.label: The impact resolved before the response began
edges.when: the condition passed on its own before anything was done
an active incident needing immediate impact reduction
an active incident where understanding comes before acting

guardrails: Severity reflects actual impact rather than event volume.
A high event count is not a severity.
The incident owner and the individual case owners remain separate.
Blast radius is re-derived as scope grows rather than fixed at confirmation.
governance.reusableRule: Incident response begins by establishing the affected scope, severity and accountable operational ownership.
governance.entityScope: the confirmed incident, its blast radius and its operational ownership
governance.entityNote: The incident owner runs the systemic response. The owners of the individual cases keep owing their customers an answer, and neither absorbs the other.

identity.title: Incident → contain and mitigate → preserve critical operations
identity.purpose: Reduce the damage now, without pretending the cause has been dealt with.

requires: an active incident with ongoing impact that could be reduced

nodes.headline: Active incident requires impact reduction

Identify the mitigations actually available - disabling a failing feature, shifting traffic, increasing capacity, moving to an alternate provider, rate limiting, a manual fallback, a degraded mode, pausing unsafe operations. Each rejected option is struck from the list, so the search through them terminates
Is the candidate mitigation safe to apply?

Reject this option, strike it from the list and consider the next. A workaround that creates a larger failure than the one it addresses is the most expensive kind of response, and it is usually applied under pressure with nobody checking what else it touches

Record that no safe mitigation is available, and say so rather than applying an unsafe one. An incident with no safe containment goes straight to recovery with its full impact visible, which is honest and is what the response should be working from

Apply the mitigation, scoped to what it actually needs to touch, and record it as temporary with the condition that would remove it. A workaround with no stated end becomes permanent by nobody's decision, and is found years later by somebody wondering why a feature is disabled

Record MITIGATED and explicitly not RESOLVED. The impact is smaller and the cause is untouched - reporting mitigation as resolution stops the investigation that would have found the cause, and the incident returns
Does the mitigation materially change what affected users should do?
Incident communication → identify affected cohort → inform, update or close
nodes.detail: a mitigation that changes user guidance

nodes.headline: Does the mitigation reduce impact enough to stand down the emergency?
MITIGATED; impact contained, cause untouched, incident still open
nodes.detail: the mitigation failing, or the impact growing past it, brings the incident back here. The mitigation stays recorded as temporary and its removal condition stays stated

nodes.headline: Recovery action → restore service → verify or continue
nodes.detail: an incident whose impact cannot be adequately contained

edges.label: Safe
edges.when: its secondary effects are understood and acceptable

edges.label: Unacceptable secondary risk
edges.when: applying it could produce a larger failure than the one it addresses

edges.label: No safe option remains
edges.when: every candidate has been considered and rejected

edges.label: It does
edges.when: a workaround is now available, or a capability is now degraded rather than absent

edges.label: It does not
edges.when: the user-visible position is unchanged
a mitigation that changes user guidance

edges.label: It does
edges.when: the remaining impact is tolerable while the cause is investigated on a normal footing

edges.label: It does not
edges.when: impact remains severe and the cause has to be acted on now
an incident whose impact cannot be adequately contained

distinctFrom.because: Mitigation reduces impact while the cause remains. INC-256 acts on the cause and asks whether the service actually came back. A system can be fully mitigated and entirely unfixed, and reporting the first as the second stops the second happening.

guardrails: Mitigated is not resolved.
A workaround never creates a larger failure than the one it addresses.
A temporary workaround remains explicitly temporary, with the condition that would remove it.
governance.reusableRule: Incident mitigation reduces current impact while preserving the distinction between temporary containment and permanent resolution.
governance.entityScope: the incident and the mitigations applied against its impact
governance.entityNote: Each mitigation is recorded as temporary with the condition that would remove it. Nothing here touches the cause.

identity.title: Incident communication → identify affected cohort → inform, update or close
identity.purpose: Tell the people actually affected something true and useful, through the mechanism that already owns delivery.

requires: an incident state change that could change what an affected party should do or expect
insufficientAlone: time having passed since the last update, which is not itself information

nodes.headline: Incident reaches communication relevant state

Determine who is materially affected, what is known, what is not known, what action the user needs to take, any safe workaround, and the condition under which the next meaningful update would happen. Saying what is not yet known is information; leaving it out and stating the rest as certainty is not
Can the affected cohort be identified with reasonable precision?

Scope the communication to the affected population. Telling everybody about an incident affecting one region trains the whole base to ignore incident notices, and the next one will be one that matters to them

Broaden only as far as necessary, and say explicitly that the scope is still being established. Uncertainty stated is information; uncertainty implied as precision is a claim that will have to be corrected
Is what would be said actually confirmed?

Say what is known and what is not, and claim nothing about cause or resolution that has not been established. A root cause announced and then retracted costs more credibility than a slow update, and technical detail stated as fact while still uncertain is the most common source of that retraction
Does this materially change the guidance the recipient already has?
Send nothing, and record why. Sending because time has passed produces noise, and noise is what makes the eventual resolution notice go unread by the people who were waiting for it
no update sent; nothing material had changed
nodes.detail: the next material change, or the next point a commitment requires an update, brings this back

nodes.headline: Raise the communication through the canonical communication mechanism, which owns the obligation, the recipient resolution, the channels, the permissions and the delivery evidence. Incident communication does not build its own delivery path, and the message carries no promotional content
Is this the resolution notice for this recipient scope?
update issued; the next update is bound to a stated condition rather than to a clock
nodes.detail: the stated condition occurring, or a material change, produces the next update

nodes.headline: resolution communicated to this recipient scope
nodes.detail: a relapse is communicated as a relapse rather than as a new incident, because the recipients were told it was over

edges.label: It can
edges.when: the affected population is identifiable by account, region, capability or cohort

edges.label: It cannot yet
edges.when: the boundary of the impact is genuinely unclear

edges.label: Confirmed
edges.when: every claim in it is established rather than believed

edges.label: Not confirmed
edges.when: the cause, the fix or the timing is still a hypothesis

edges.label: It does
edges.when: what they should do, expect or avoid has changed

edges.label: It does not, and no commitment requires an update
edges.when: nothing has changed for them since the last message

edges.label: It does
edges.when: what they should do, expect or avoid has changed

edges.label: It is
edges.when: the incident is resolved for the population this message goes to

edges.label: It is not
edges.when: the incident continues for them

guardrails: No root cause or resolution is claimed before it is confirmed.
No promotional content appears in incident communication.
Uncertain technical detail is never communicated as fact.
The affected cohort is identified as precisely as the evidence allows.
governance.reusableRule: Incident communication should provide verified, actionable information to the population actually affected by the incident.
governance.entityScope: the incident, the affected recipient cohort and the communication obligation it creates
governance.entityNote: This decides what should be said and to whom. Channels, permissions, delivery and retries belong to the communication lifecycle.

identity.title: Root cause investigation → hypothesis → confirm or reject → corrective action
identity.purpose: Find the thing that actually explains the incident, rather than the thing that was nearest to it.

requires: a confirmed incident whose cause is not established
insufficientAlone: the incident having a trigger, which is what set it off rather than what made it possible

nodes.headline: Incident requires causal investigation

Collect the timeline, the logs and evidence, the change history, the dependency state, the affected cohort, the failure signatures and the effects the mitigations had. What a mitigation did or did not fix is itself evidence about the cause

Form hypotheses that would explain the whole incident rather than its first symptom. The change that shipped just before an incident is the most available explanation and is frequently not the cause - often it is what made a latent problem visible, and fixing it leaves the problem in place

Test the current hypothesis against the evidence, including the parts of the evidence it does not explain. A hypothesis that accounts for most of an incident and not its timing, or not its cohort, has not been confirmed
Does the evidence support this hypothesis?

Reject the hypothesis and record why, so the next investigator does not retest it. Correlation is not causation, and a condition present during an incident that nothing connects to the failure is a coincidence that will be treated as an answer unless it is rejected explicitly
Are hypotheses left to test?

Record the incident as unexplained rather than attributing it to the most plausible remaining candidate. An unexplained incident is a known gap somebody can work on; a wrongly attributed one is a closed question that will reopen as the same incident with everybody convinced it was fixed
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: an incident no available hypothesis explains

nodes.headline: Record ROOT_CAUSE_CONFIRMED with the evidence supporting it and exactly what it explains. Service may already have been restored - restoration and understanding proceed independently, and holding one for the other extends an outage for the sake of tidiness

Define the corrective action the confirmed cause implies, separately from whatever mitigation is currently holding the impact down. The mitigation is a workaround; this is the thing that makes the workaround unnecessary
Recovery action → restore service → verify or continue
nodes.detail: a confirmed cause with a defined corrective action

edges.label: Supported and it explains the incident
edges.when: it accounts for the failure, its timing, its cohort and its behaviour under mitigation

edges.label: Not supported
edges.when: the evidence contradicts it or leaves it unexplained

edges.label: Not supported
edges.when: the evidence contradicts it or leaves it unexplained

edges.label: Some remain
edges.when: the list has untested candidates

edges.label: None explains it
edges.when: every candidate within the investigation's bounds has been tested and rejected
an incident no available hypothesis explains
a confirmed cause with a defined corrective action

guardrails: The first plausible explanation is not the root cause.
Correlation is not causation.
The root cause remains evidence-based rather than assigned by elimination.
Service may be restored before the root cause is known.
governance.reusableRule: Root cause is established through evidence that explains the incident, not merely through the first condition correlated with failure.
governance.entityScope: the incident and the investigation into what caused it
governance.entityNote: Hypotheses are a finite list, tested one at a time. Rejections are recorded so the next investigator does not retest them.

identity.title: Recovery action → restore service → verify or continue
identity.purpose: Act on the cause and then check the affected population, not the command's return code.

requires: an authorized corrective or recovery action against an active incident

nodes.headline: Recovery action authorized
Execute the corrective action against the affected scope, through the canonical execution and reliability primitives rather than a bespoke path built during the incident
until the action reports applied, or the action reports a failure
nodes.detail: timeout after the action's execution window

nodes.headline: Record the action's outcome as unknown and hold further attempts. Applying a second recovery action on top of one that may have landed is how an incident gets a second cause
external:external-status-reconciliation
nodes.detail: a recovery action whose outcome could not be established

nodes.headline: Did the action apply?

Verify from the affected population rather than from the action's own success - service availability, error rates, critical transactions, business functions, dependency health, and the recovery of the cohort that was actually affected. A recovery command succeeding says the command ran, and one successful synthetic check says one path works for one caller
Is service restored across the affected population?

Keep the incident active and name the unresolved scope explicitly. A partial restoration reported as recovery leaves the remaining population inside an incident everybody has stopped watching, which is how a long tail of affected customers goes unnoticed for days
Is another recovery action available?
Take the next action from the response's defined list. The list is finite, so attempts progress through it and terminate rather than cycling on the same action with different hopes
external:human-in-the-loop-lifecycle
nodes.detail: an incident whose defined recovery actions are exhausted

nodes.headline: Record RECOVERY_OBSERVED. What has been established is that the affected population works now - not that it will still be working in an hour, which is the next question and a different one
Service restored → observation window → stable or relapse
nodes.detail: service observed restored across the affected population

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the action reports applied, the action reports a failure

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: an action whose outcome is unknown may or may not have changed the system, and the next decision depends entirely on which
a recovery action whose outcome could not be established

edges.label: Applied
edges.when: the corrective action completed against the affected scope

edges.label: Failed
edges.when: the action itself did not complete

edges.label: Restored
edges.when: the affected cohort's real traffic succeeds and the critical functions work

edges.label: Partially restored
edges.when: some of the affected population works and some does not

edges.label: Not restored
edges.when: the action applied and the impact continues

edges.label: One remains
edges.when: the response defines a further corrective action that has not been attempted

edges.label: None
edges.when: the defined actions are exhausted
an incident whose defined recovery actions are exhausted
service observed restored across the affected population

guardrails: A recovery command succeeding is not service restored.
One successful synthetic check does not prove population recovery.
Partial restoration stays explicit and keeps the incident active.
governance.reusableRule: Incident recovery becomes meaningful only when the affected service and user population demonstrate restored operation.
governance.entityScope: the incident, the recovery action and the capability it is meant to restore
governance.entityNote: The recovery actions available are a finite list defined by the response. Attempts progress through it rather than repeating indefinitely.

identity.title: Service restored → observation window → stable or relapse
identity.purpose: Hold the incident open long enough to know the recovery held.

requires: verified restoration across the affected population
insufficientAlone: a recovery action completing, which is what produced the signal rather than the signal itself

nodes.headline: Material recovery observed

Record RECOVERY_OBSERVATION. The incident is not resolved - recoveries that hold for ten minutes and fail again are common, and closing on the first good signal means reopening in front of the same customers who were just told it was over

Set the observation window from the incident's own character - how long the failure took to manifest, how often the affected path runs, and whether the fix addressed a cause or a symptom. A fixed window applied to every incident is either too long for a trivial one or far too short for one on a rare path
until the same failure returns, or new affected cases appear
nodes.detail: timeout after the observation window set for this incident

nodes.headline: What appeared during observation?

Return the incident to ACTIVE. What resumes is this incident rather than a new one - the recurrence is evidence about the recovery, and opening a fresh incident hides that the fix did not hold and makes the pattern invisible
Incident → contain and mitigate → preserve critical operations
nodes.detail: a recovery that did not hold

nodes.headline: Assess it separately rather than absorbing it into this incident. Attaching every failure that occurs during an observation window to the incident makes the incident unfalsifiable - it can never be shown to have ended
an unrelated failure raised separately; this observation continues on its own terms
nodes.detail: if the separate assessment shows the two do share a cause, they are correlated on that evidence rather than on having overlapped in time

nodes.headline: Record STABLE_RECOVERY with what was observed and for how long. The observation is part of the record, because the next similar incident's window is set against it
Incident resolution → close operational response → preserve residual cases
nodes.detail: a recovery that held through its observation window

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the same failure returns, new affected cases appear

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: reaching the window without recurrence is what makes the recovery stable. Holding it open longer without need keeps a response engaged on something that has finished

edges.label: The same failure returned
edges.when: the incident's own signature recurs in the affected population

edges.label: New cases, a different failure
edges.when: something else is failing during the window
a recovery that did not hold
a recovery that held through its observation window

distinctFrom.because: RET-27 buffers one relationship's recovery signal before concluding the relationship is healthy. This applies the same principle to a shared operational failure - same discipline, different entity, and here a relapse returns a population to an incident rather than a person to a risk state.

guardrails: Service restored once is not the incident resolved.
The observation duration and evidence reflect the incident's type rather than a standard.
Observation is not kept artificially long without need.
governance.reusableRule: Initial restoration should enter an observation state until sufficient evidence shows the recovery is stable.
governance.entityScope: the incident and the recovered service under observation
governance.entityNote: The window is set from the incident's own character rather than from a standard duration.

identity.title: Incident resolution → close operational response → preserve residual cases
identity.purpose: Close the shared failure without closing the individual problems it caused.

requires: a stable recovery and the incident's own resolution criteria met
insufficientAlone: service being restored, which is one of the criteria rather than all of them

nodes.headline: Incident resolution criteria satisfied

Mark the systemic incident RESOLVED, preserving its timeline, its mitigations and every decision taken during it. The record is what the review works from and what any later recurrence is compared against - an incident that keeps only its outcome teaches nothing
Stop the incident-specific emergency operations - the elevated monitoring, the standing bridge, the suspended changes. These have their own cost and they end with the incident rather than drifting on
What happens to the temporary mitigations?

Remove them and verify the service holds without them. A mitigation left in place because removing it is frightening becomes permanent by nobody's decision, and it joins the set of quietly permanent emergency controls that is the least-understood part of most systems
Formalize it explicitly as a change with an owner and a rationale, rather than leaving a temporary control quietly running forever. Every one of those was meant to last an afternoon
Do individual affected cases remain unresolved?

Detach them and let each continue on its own recovery. The systemic cause is fixed and the customer whose order failed still has a failed order - closing their case because the incident closed tells them the problem is solved at exactly the moment they discover it is not
Do financial or remedy obligations remain from the incident?
Remedy selection → resolve obligation → financial handoff if needed
nodes.detail: obligations surviving an incident's closure

nodes.headline: Does this incident qualify for a post-incident review?
Post-incident review → learn → corrective work → verify
nodes.detail: a resolved incident qualifying for review

nodes.headline: RESOLVED; the shared failure closed and its record preserved
nodes.detail: a recurrence is correlated against this record rather than assessed from nothing, which is what makes a pattern visible across incidents

edges.label: Safe to remove
edges.when: the corrective action makes them unnecessary

edges.label: They should become permanent
edges.when: the mitigation turned out to be the right long-term behaviour

edges.label: Some remain
edges.when: linked entity-level problems are still outstanding

edges.label: None
edges.when: every linked case has independently reached resolution

edges.label: Some remain
edges.when: refunds, credits, compensation or unmet service obligations were created by the incident

edges.label: None
edges.when: nothing is owed as a result of it
obligations surviving an incident's closure

edges.label: It does
edges.when: its severity, novelty or recurrence meets the threshold for review

edges.label: It does not
edges.when: it falls below the review threshold and nothing about it was novel
a resolved incident qualifying for review

guardrails: An incident resolved is not every individual case resolved.
Temporary mitigations do not silently become permanent.
Incident closure preserves the timeline and the decisions taken.
governance.reusableRule: Incident resolution closes the shared systemic failure while leaving entity-specific obligations open until they independently reach resolution.
governance.entityScope: the incident and the individual cases and obligations linked to it
governance.entityNote: The incident's resolution is a statement about the shared cause. Every linked case reaches its own resolution on its own terms.

identity.title: Post-incident review → learn → corrective work → verify
identity.purpose: Turn what the incident showed into work somebody owns and somebody checks.

requires: a resolved incident meeting the threshold for post-incident review

nodes.headline: Incident qualifies for review

Review the timeline, the detection, the response, the root cause, the blast radius, the mitigations, the communication, the recovery, the control failures and the near misses. What is examined is the system and the response rather than the people - a review that finds a person found the wrong thing, because the person will move on and the condition will not

Identify the corrective and preventive actions the evidence actually supports. An action nobody can trace to something the incident revealed is a good idea rather than a finding, and mixing the two makes the real findings harder to prioritise
Does the review produce corrective work?

Record explicitly that the review found no corrective work required, with the reasoning. That is a legitimate outcome and it needs to be a stated one rather than an empty section that reads as an unfinished review
reviewed; no outstanding corrective work
nodes.detail: a recurrence reopens the question of whether the conclusion that nothing needed changing was right

nodes.headline: Assign owners and deadlines to each corrective action. An action item with no owner is a sentence in a document, and a document is not a control - the whole value of the review is what somebody is now accountable for delivering
until the required corrective actions are claimed complete, or corrective actions are abandoned or superseded
nodes.detail: timeout after the deadlines assigned to the corrective actions

nodes.headline: Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: corrective work outliving its assigned deadline

nodes.headline: What happened to the corrective work?

Record which actions were dropped and on whose authority. Silently abandoned prevention work is the reason the same incident recurs, and without this record nobody can point to the moment it was dropped or ask why

Verify the corrective work where verification is required. An action item created is not a risk reduced, and a document published is not a prevention - what is checked is whether the condition that produced the incident can still produce it
Did the corrective work actually reduce the risk?
Return the action to its owner with what the verification found. Work completed that did not reduce the risk means the action was aimed at the wrong thing, and repeating it produces the same result
Record the corrective work as complete and verified, with what the verification established
review closed with verified corrective work
nodes.detail: a recurrence despite verified prevention is strong evidence the diagnosis was wrong, and is assessed at pattern level rather than as a fresh incident

edges.label: It does
edges.when: the evidence supports specific preventive or corrective actions

edges.label: It does not
edges.when: the response worked, the controls held, and nothing the incident revealed needs changing

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the required corrective actions are claimed complete, corrective actions are abandoned or superseded

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: prevention work that slips past its deadline unremarked is how the same incident recurs, and by then nobody remembers the action existed
corrective work outliving its assigned deadline

edges.label: Claimed complete
edges.when: the owners report the actions done

edges.label: Abandoned or superseded
edges.when: the actions were dropped or replaced

edges.label: Verified
edges.when: the condition the incident exposed can no longer produce it

edges.label: Not effective
edges.when: the work completed and the condition remains reachable

guardrails: A postmortem is not a blame exercise.
An action item created is not a risk reduced.
Prevention is never marked complete solely because a document was published.
governance.reusableRule: Post-incident review converts incident evidence into owned, verifiable improvements rather than treating documentation itself as remediation.
governance.entityScope: the resolved incident and the corrective work its review produces
governance.entityNote: The review's output is owned work with deadlines. A published document is not a control and is not the deliverable.

identity.title: Incident pattern recurrence → detect systemic weakness → escalate prevention
identity.purpose: Notice when the same weakness keeps producing incidents, and stop treating each one as new.
