nodes.detail: reaching the point where a person is required opens assignment; the queue is an owner, recorded as one rather than as an empty field

edges.label: Already owned
edges.when: an active assignment exists on this item

edges.label: Unowned
edges.when: no active assignment exists

edges.label: Route determined
edges.when: the routing rules resolve to a specific owner, team or queue

edges.label: No route
edges.when: the rules do not resolve, or no rule covers this case

edges.label: Named owner required
edges.when: the work cannot proceed, or its SLA cannot run, without a specific person responsible

edges.label: Queue ownership is enough
edges.when: the queue itself carries responsibility until the work reaches the point where a person picks it up
work needing a named owner

distinctFrom.because: This decides where the work belongs. OWN-52 decides whether the person it landed on has taken it, which is a different state and frequently a different answer.

guardrails: Where the routing rule is unknown, no priority logic is invented to stand in for it. The item goes to the fallback and says why.
The assignment reason and its inputs are preserved, so a route that is consistently wrong can be found.
One item does not acquire two active owners from duplicate routing events, unless a multi-owner model is explicitly defined for that work type.
governance.reusableRule: Work should enter the smallest valid responsibility scope before execution begins.
governance.entityScope: the individual work item - a case, lead, opportunity, task or request
governance.entityNote: One item, one active routing. A duplicate routing event is not a second assignment, and treating it as one produces two people doing the same work differently.

identity.title: Assignment → acceptance → active responsibility
identity.purpose: Keep proposed responsibility and accepted responsibility as different states, so work nobody has taken is visible as such.

requires: an assignment naming a specific person as proposed owner
insufficientAlone: a notification delivered to that person, which is delivery and not agreement
the item appearing in their queue view

nodes.headline: Work assigned to named owner
Record the state as ASSIGNED - proposed responsibility. Nothing that requires an active owner may proceed on this state, which is the entire reason it is distinct from the next one
Does this work type require explicit acceptance?
until the owner accepts, or the owner rejects
nodes.detail: timeout after the acceptance SLA for this work type

nodes.headline: What did the proposed owner do?
Capture why it was rejected. The reason is routing information - wrong expertise, wrong region, conflict of interest, capacity - and it is what stops the next route repeating the mistake
Invalidate anything the un-accepted assignment queued, so nothing goes out under an ownership that was never taken
Work created → routing → assignment
nodes.detail: an assignment that was not taken

nodes.headline: With the acceptance SLA passed, what does policy do?
Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: an assignment unanswered past its SLA

nodes.headline: Record ACTIVE_OWNERSHIP. From here the owner is answerable for the work, and the distinction from ASSIGNED is what makes that statement true rather than assumed
Owner assignment → context transfer → work start
nodes.detail: responsibility becoming active

edges.label: Acceptance required
edges.when: policy or the nature of the work means responsibility has to be taken rather than allocated

edges.label: Assignment is sufficient
edges.when: policy allocates this work type directly, and the owner is responsible on assignment

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the owner accepts, the owner rejects

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: an assignment nobody has answered is not owned, and letting it sit unanswered is how work becomes invisible while appearing allocated

edges.label: Accepted
edges.when: they took responsibility

edges.label: Rejected
edges.when: they declined it
an assignment that was not taken

edges.label: Escalate
edges.when: policy raises unanswered assignments rather than moving them

edges.label: Reassign
edges.when: policy reroutes an assignment that was not answered in time
an assignment unanswered past its SLA
responsibility becoming active

guardrails: Assigned is not accepted. A report counting assignments as owned work is counting proposals.
A notification delivered to an owner is not responsibility accepted. Delivery is a fact about a message.
Reassignment invalidates the previous owner's pending actions rather than leaving them to fire under an ownership that ended.
governance.reusableRule: Assignment creates proposed responsibility; acceptance establishes active responsibility when acceptance is required.
governance.entityScope: the work item plus this specific assignment of it
governance.entityNote: Each assignment is its own record. A rejected one and the reassignment that follows are two facts, and the first is routing information worth keeping.

identity.title: Owner assignment → context transfer → work start
identity.purpose: Give a new owner what they need to continue an existing obligation, rather than an entity with their name on it.

requires: a valid ownership assignment taking effect on an entity with existing state

nodes.headline: Owner assignment became effective

Assemble what the owner needs to continue: the current state, the open obligations, the deadlines running against them, decisions already taken, the history bearing on those decisions, pending dependencies, and anything promised to anyone
Does that context include sensitive data this owner does not need?
Transfer what the work requires and no more. A handover is not a reason to widen who can see something, and the fact that it moved with the case is not a justification anyone will accept later
Does policy require the owner to acknowledge critical items?
until the owner acknowledges the critical items
nodes.detail: timeout after a bounded acknowledgement window

nodes.headline: Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: critical context left unacknowledged

nodes.headline: The owner begins from the current authoritative state. The entity's lifecycle is not restarted, its history is not cleared, and the previous owners remain in the chain - a new owner is a continuation, not a first contact
owner working from current state with inherited context
nodes.detail: the next ownership change opens its own transfer

edges.label: More than needed
edges.when: the history contains personal, health, financial or confidential detail beyond what the work requires

edges.label: Proportionate
edges.when: the context is what the work requires and no more

edges.label: Acknowledgement required
edges.when: there are commitments or deadlines whose transfer has to be confirmed rather than assumed

edges.label: Not required
edges.when: the context transfers without a confirmation step

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the owner acknowledges the critical items

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: unacknowledged critical context is the state in which a deadline is missed by someone who did not know it existed
critical context left unacknowledged

distinctFrom.because: OWN-52 establishes that someone has taken responsibility. This establishes that they can actually discharge it, which fails independently and more quietly.

guardrails: A new owner does not restart the lifecycle. The obligation is older than their involvement in it.
Assignment appends to the ownership chain rather than overwriting who held it before.
Context transfer is proportionate. Sensitive detail does not travel simply because it was attached to the case.
governance.reusableRule: Ownership becomes operationally useful only when the new owner inherits the context required to continue the existing obligation.
governance.entityScope: the business entity plus the owner now responsible for it
governance.entityNote: The entity's history belongs to the entity, not to whoever currently holds it. Ownership changes what the record points at, never what it contains.

identity.title: Ownership change → transfer obligations → continue
identity.purpose: Move responsibility for an active entity without losing anything that was already owed, without letting the clock restart, and without rewriting who did what before the change.

requires: a recorded change of owner on an entity with active obligations

nodes.headline: Authoritative ownership change
Record the previous owner, the next owner, the reason and the effective time, appended to the ownership chain

Leave every historical action, decision, payment, document, approval and obligation attributed exactly as it occurred. This is done first rather than last, because everything after it is tempted to rewrite it - and a new owner appearing as the author of last year's approvals produces a record that is not merely wrong but actively misleading to anyone auditing it

Identify everything still open and everything that depends on who the owner is: tasks, commitments, deadlines, live escalations, follow-ups promised to people, decisions pending, access, responsibilities, pending approvals, notifications, billing and administrative contacts, assigned work, delegations and external representations. Every deadline carries across unchanged - a commitment made to someone outside the organisation does not move because we moved who holds it internally

Invalidate the previous owner's queued actions that they are clearly no longer authorised to take. An action scheduled under an ownership that has ended and delivered afterwards comes from someone who is not responsible any more, and neither the recipient nor the new owner will know that. Actions that may still be valid are not invalidated here - they are held and revalidated once the transfer completes
Does the incoming owner have to accept the transfer?
until the incoming owner accepts, or the incoming owner declines
nodes.detail: timeout after the transfer acceptance window

nodes.headline: Did the incoming owner take it?
The transfer did not complete - what does policy provide?
Assign the fallback owner and record that the intended transfer failed, so the fallback is visible as a fallback rather than as the original plan

Take each owner-dependent item from the inventory in turn - access, responsibilities, pending approvals, notifications, billing and administrative contacts, assigned work, delegations, external representations - and establish what it actually attaches to
Does this dependency belong to the entity or to the person who owned it?
Move it to the current owner. A billing contact, an administrative notification and an escalation path follow whoever is accountable now, because that is what they were always pointing at

Leave it with the previous owner. Contracts, payments and obligations frequently belong to the entity rather than to its owner, and just as frequently the reverse - each is evaluated rather than moved by default, because moving one wrongly transfers a liability nobody agreed to take on
Is any pending action authorised only by the previous ownership state?

Hold it and revalidate before execution. An action approved by somebody who is no longer the owner is an authorisation whose basis has gone, and executing it applies a decision the current owner never made and may not have made
Does any delegation depend on the previous owner's authority?
Delegation revoked → remove delegated authority → preserve independent access
nodes.detail: delegations derived from an authority that has changed hands

nodes.headline: Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: a transfer that failed with no fallback

nodes.headline: Owner assignment → context transfer → work start
nodes.detail: ownership successfully moved

edges.label: Acceptance required
edges.when: policy requires the new owner to take it rather than receive it

edges.label: Transfer is effective directly
edges.when: policy moves ownership without a confirmation step, or the cutover has already completed elsewhere

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the incoming owner accepts, the incoming owner declines

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: an unanswered transfer leaves the entity between two owners, which is the one state in which nobody is responsible while the record says somebody is

edges.label: Accepted
edges.when: they accepted the transfer

edges.label: Declined
edges.when: they declined it

edges.label: A fallback owner
edges.when: policy names a fallback for failed transfers

edges.label: No fallback
edges.when: no fallback is defined

edges.label: To the entity
edges.when: it exists because the entity has an owner rather than because of who that owner was

edges.label: To the previous owner personally
edges.when: it is theirs - a personal commitment, a personal obligation, an individually held right

edges.label: There is
edges.when: an approval, an instruction or a scheduled change rests on the previous owner's authority

edges.label: There is not
edges.when: nothing outstanding depends on who the owner was

edges.label: One or more do
edges.when: delegations were granted by the previous owner out of authority they no longer hold

edges.label: None
edges.when: no live delegation derives from the previous owner
delegations derived from an authority that has changed hands
a transfer that failed with no fallback
ownership successfully moved

guardrails: A transfer never resets an inherited deadline or commitment. Only an explicit renegotiation of the obligation itself does that, and that is a different event with a different record.
Stale actions from the former owner do not execute after the transfer.
The historical owner chain is preserved in full.
Work is never silently orphaned. A failed transfer escalates rather than leaving a null owner.
An ownership change is not a rewrite of historical attribution: past actions, decisions, payments, documents and approvals stay attributed to whoever performed them.
Pending responsibilities are never transferred blindly; each is evaluated for whether it follows the entity or the person.
Contracts and financial obligations may belong to the entity rather than to its owner and are evaluated separately.
governance.reusableRule: Ownership changes who is responsible for an obligation; they do not create a new obligation or reset its history.
governance.entityScope: the business entity, its previous owner and its next one
governance.entityNote: Three parties in the record. The chain is what makes it possible to say who was responsible at the time something did or did not happen.

identity.title: Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
identity.purpose: Move a blocker up to the level that can clear it, without the original owner putting the work down by raising it.

requires: a defined escalation condition: an SLA breached or at risk, an authority limit reached, a severity threshold crossed, a blocker the owner cannot clear, repeated failed resolution, or an explicit requirement to escalate
insufficientAlone: an owner finding the work difficult
elapsed time with no defined SLA behind it

nodes.headline: Escalation condition met
Capture why it is escalating and the current context, so the higher authority is deciding rather than re-discovering the case
Does policy define a valid escalation destination for this?
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: an escalation with no defined destination

nodes.headline: Does escalating transfer ownership, or ask for a decision?
Ownership change → transfer obligations → continue
nodes.detail: an escalation that genuinely moves ownership

nodes.headline: Record that the original owner remains responsible while the higher authority is asked for a decision or support. Escalating is not putting the work down, and the record has to say so or the case falls between two people who each believe the other has it
until a decision is provided, or the blocker is resolved
nodes.detail: timeout after the escalation SLA at this level

nodes.headline: What did the higher authority produce?
blocker cleared; the original owner continues
nodes.detail: nothing is handed back, because nothing was handed over - the owner has been responsible throughout and now has what they were missing

nodes.headline: resolved at the escalated level
nodes.detail: a recurrence is a new escalation, judged with this one in the history

nodes.headline: Is there a further escalation level that has not been used?
Escalate one level further and record the level. The ladder is walked once - a loop that keeps re-escalating to the same place is how an unresolvable case stays busy without moving
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: work outliving the whole escalation ladder

edges.label: Defined
edges.when: an escalation path exists for this work type and condition

edges.label: Undefined
edges.when: no escalation path covers this case
an escalation with no defined destination

edges.label: Ownership moves
edges.when: policy says the higher authority takes the work rather than advising on it

edges.label: Decision or support only
edges.when: the original owner stays responsible and needs a decision, an authority, or help
an escalation that genuinely moves ownership

edges.label: on event
edges.when: a decision is provided, the blocker is resolved

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: an escalation that produces nothing is itself a blocker, and it is the one the original owner cannot escalate around

edges.label: Unblocked, work continues
edges.when: the decision or support clears the blocker and the work goes on

edges.label: Resolved outright
edges.when: the higher authority's decision closes the work itself

edges.label: Level remains
edges.when: the policy's ladder has another rung

edges.label: Ladder exhausted
edges.when: every defined level has been tried
work outliving the whole escalation ladder

distinctFrom.because: Escalation is usually a request for a decision, not a handover. Where it does move ownership, it hands to OWN-54 to do that properly rather than doing it as a side effect.

guardrails: Escalation is not abandonment. Unless ownership explicitly transfers, the original owner remains responsible throughout.
The escalation path comes from policy. Where none is defined, none is invented.
Repeated escalation is bounded by the ladder rather than by patience.

An exhausted ladder closes as an operational exception with no customer-facing message. The person on the other end of the work is owed an outcome from whoever picks it up, not a notification that our escalation ran out.

Escalation is an internal operational state throughout. Reaching a level creates no customer communication by itself; a message goes out only where a separate communication obligation exists for it, and an internal delay is not news about what the customer wants.

Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold

nodes.headline: Are the independence rules between the required authorities defined?

Build the approval graph from the policy - parallel, sequential, or whatever structure it defines - together with the threshold the policy sets, and bind the package to the exact action and subject version it authorises. Record which policy defined it, so the aggregation can be explained and audited rather than merely trusted
until the required decision set resolves, or a blocking rejection arrives, or changes are requested by any approver, or the action or subject version changes underneath the package
nodes.detail: timeout after the approval SLA for the package

nodes.headline: Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: a decision set left incomplete past its SLA

nodes.headline: What does the policy say about the decisions received?

Re-evaluate the collected decisions against the changed action and version, and discard any that no longer apply. Approvals bind to a version - an approval given for one amount does not carry to a larger one, and carrying it forward is how a threshold gets met for something nobody approved

Verify each counted decision came from a genuinely distinct authority under the policy's independence rules. The same person approving through two roles is one authority counted twice, and it is by far the most common way a two-person rule is satisfied by one person
Are the counted decisions genuinely independent?

Record that the threshold was not genuinely met, naming the duplicate authority, and keep waiting. The count looked satisfied and was not, and saying which decisions collapsed is what lets somebody find a genuinely independent approver rather than re-reading the same one
Record the authorisation as blocked, naming the rejection that blocked it. One approval among several is never read as approval by all required parties
authorisation blocked by a decision the policy treats as blocking
nodes.detail: a revised version may be submitted where the policy permits it; the blocking decision stays in the record either way

revision required; affected decisions re-opened, unaffected ones retained
nodes.detail: the revised version enters as its own package with the retained decisions carried forward

nodes.detail: the governing policy's decision set being satisfied

a decision set left incomplete past its SLA

edges.when: an approver requires a different version

edges.label: The action or version changed underneath the package
edges.when: what is being authorised is no longer what the collected decisions were given against

edges.when: the policy's threshold and condition for a complete decision set are met

edges.label: Not independent

the governing policy's decision set being satisfied

guardrails: Aggregation logic comes from the governing policy. Majority, unanimity, quorum, tie-breaks and any n-of-m rule are never inferred, and where none is defined the journey stops rather than choosing one.
One approval is not approval by all required parties.
Sequential dependencies are respected where the policy defines them.
A materially revised subject re-opens the decisions whose basis it changed, and only those.
Multiple administrators are not multi-party authorization.
The same authority is never counted twice where independence is required.
Collected decisions bind to the same action and version; a changed action re-opens the threshold.
governance.reusableRule: Multi-party authorization is complete only when the governing decision policy says the required decision set has been satisfied.
governance.entityScope: the approval package, the action and subject version it authorises, and each authority's individual decision
governance.entityNote: Each decision is its own record against its own version. Aggregation reads them; it never replaces them. Several people holding access is not multi-party authorization - the requirement is that distinct authorities approve the same specific thing.

identity.title: Material change after approval → impact check → re-approval or continue
identity.purpose: Work out whether an approval still covers what the subject has become, and re-open only the decisions whose basis stopped being true.

Compare the approved version with the current one and establish exactly what changed - value, scope, quantity, discount, destination, risk profile, commercial terms, a critical configuration, or something none of those cover
Does policy define what counts as material for this subject?
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold

nodes.headline: Is the change material to the basis on which approval was given?
existing approval remains valid
nodes.detail: a further change is compared against the same approved version - minor edits accumulating into a material difference is exactly what this comparison is for

nodes.headline: Identify which approvals rested on the part that changed. An unrelated approval on the same subject is untouched - invalidating everything on every material change teaches approvers that re-approval is routine, which is how it stops being read
Invalidate those approvals, keeping them in the history as approvals that were validly given and then superseded. The original decision is not deleted; it stops applying
Is execution pending that would now proceed without valid approval?
Hold the affected execution. Only the affected part - holding everything because one term changed is the same error as invalidating every approval
Request re-approval, scoped to the authorities whose basis actually changed rather than to everyone who approved the original
until the required re-approvals resolve
nodes.detail: timeout after the re-approval SLA

nodes.headline: Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: re-approval left outstanding past its SLA with execution held

nodes.headline: Was the changed version approved?
current version approved; held execution may resume
nodes.detail: any further change is compared against this newly approved version

nodes.detail: a changed version failing re-approval

edges.label: Defined
edges.when: a materiality rule exists for this kind of subject and change

edges.label: Not defined
edges.when: no rule says whether this change matters
a change whose materiality no policy defines

edges.when: the required re-approvals resolve

edges.when: held execution is not free - it is a commitment sitting still - so an unanswered re-approval escalates rather than waiting indefinitely

edges.label: Not approved

guardrails: A minor edit does not reset every approval. Only those whose decision basis stopped being true are invalidated.
Materiality is defined by policy, not decided here. Where no rule exists the journey stops and asks.
The approval history is preserved. A superseded approval is recorded as superseded, not removed.
Re-approval is scoped to the affected authority wherever the policy allows it.
governance.reusableRule: Material changes should invalidate only the approvals whose original decision assumptions are no longer true.
governance.entityScope: the approved subject, its version history and the approvals bound to those versions
governance.entityNote: Approvals are bound to versions, which is what makes this question answerable at all. Without the binding there is nothing to compare the current state against.

identity.title: Approval rejected → revision eligibility → resubmit or close
identity.purpose: Keep rejection from being either a dead end by default or a retry loop, and make sure a rejected version cannot quietly execute later.

requires: a recorded rejection against a specific approval request and subject version

nodes.headline: Approval rejected
Capture the rejection reason against the exact version rejected, appended. The history of what was rejected and why is what makes an unchanged resubmission recognisable as one

Mark the rejected version as not executable. A rejected version executing later because something downstream read the subject and not the decision is the quietest failure in this category and the hardest to notice afterwards
Does policy allow this to be revised and resubmitted?
rejected, no revision path
nodes.detail: none - what would have to change is the rule or the circumstances, and either of those produces a new request rather than a revision of this one

nodes.headline: Identify what would actually have to change, taken from the rejection reason rather than left to the requester to guess
until the subject is revised
nodes.detail: timeout after the revision window

nodes.headline: revision window closed; request expired
nodes.detail: a genuinely new request may be raised later, with this rejection in its history

nodes.headline: Does the revision materially address what was rejected?
resubmission refused; nothing material changed
nodes.detail: a real revision re-opens this. Sending the same thing back is not a revision, and letting it through is how approval becomes a queue people learn to clear rather than read

nodes.headline: Create the new reviewable version, linked to the rejected one and its reason, so the reviewer can see what was asked for and what changed
Approval request → review → approve, reject or request changes
nodes.detail: a genuine revision of a rejected subject

edges.label: Revision permitted
edges.when: policy provides a revision path for this rejection reason

edges.label: Terminal

edges.when: the subject is revised

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a rejected request left open indefinitely is a commitment nobody is tracking and a queue entry nobody will clear

edges.label: Unchanged in substance

a genuine revision of a rejected subject

guardrails: A rejected version is marked unexecutable and never runs later.
An unchanged resubmission is refused. Repetition is not a revision.
The rejection history is preserved and travels with the revised version.
governance.reusableRule: A rejected decision can re-enter approval only through a valid revision path when policy permits it.
governance.entityScope: the rejected approval request and the exact subject version it rejected
governance.entityNote: The rejection belongs to a version. A later version is a different subject and is judged on its own; this one stays rejected permanently.

identity.title: Decision authority change → revalidate pending decisions → transfer or continue
identity.purpose: Re-evaluate decisions against who is actually authorised now, without unapproving history or blindly moving what is pending.

requires: a change to who holds decision authority: an approver leaving, a role change, authority revoked, organisational responsibility moving, an approval limit changing, or a delegation beginning or ending

nodes.headline: Decision authority changed

Identify what this touches: decisions still pending, decisions already made, deadlines running, and the exact scope of authority that changed. The scope matters - a lowered approval limit affects a different set from a departure
Invalidate anything queued that the former authority is no longer entitled to do, so a decision does not arrive from someone who has stopped being able to make it
Are pending decisions now sitting with an authority that is no longer valid?
Does a valid alternative authority exist?

Reassign the pending decision, preserving the original request, the exact version under review and the deadline. The clock does not restart because we changed who is reading it - the requester's wait is not reset by our reorganisation
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a decision with no currently valid authority

nodes.headline: Do decisions already made remain valid under the governing policy?
completed decisions retained; pending ones reassigned where needed
nodes.detail: an approver leaving does not retroactively unapprove what they approved while they held the authority to approve it

nodes.headline: Identify which completed decisions this change actually invalidates, and only those. A new authority does not inherit the ability to reopen decisions outside their scope simply by arriving
Approval request → review → approve, reject or request changes

guardrails: An approver's departure does not automatically invalidate every historical approval they gave.
A new authority does not inherit the ability to alter completed decisions outside what policy grants them.
An authority change does not reset the original request history or its SLA unless policy explicitly says so.
Where no valid authority exists, execution requiring approval stays blocked rather than proceeding because nobody is left to refuse it.

Does establishing this relationship require verification or acceptance by either party?
Verification requirement → collect evidence → resume blocked process

PENDING_EVIDENCE; the relationship is not active
nodes.detail: sufficient basis arriving later activates it. Nothing flows from a pending relationship, which is the difference between pending and active

nodes.headline: REJECTED; no relationship created
nodes.detail: a different basis is assessed on its own terms

ACTIVE_RELATIONSHIP
nodes.detail: changes to it are REL-92's, and its ending is REL-93's

edges.label: Verification or acceptance required
edges.when: the relationship confers rights, responsibility or visibility that one side has to agree to

edges.label: Neither required
edges.when: the relationship is administrative and confers nothing that needs consent
a relationship whose creation depends on verification or acceptance

edges.when: the basis is sufficient and the relationship is permitted between these entity types

edges.when: the relationship is plausible and the basis is not yet sufficient

edges.label: Not valid
edges.when: the relationship is not permitted, or the basis contradicts it

distinctFrom.because: This establishes that a relationship exists. REL-98 defines what a link between two entities is allowed to share, which is a separate decision that many relationships answer with nothing.

SUB-161 creates a relationship that carries a term - an effective date, a renewal model and terms that can lapse. This creates a structural link between two entities, which can exist indefinitely without any of those. An employee belongs to an organisation here; the organisation's contract is created there, and the two end for different reasons on different days.

guardrails: A shared attribute is not proof of a relationship. Two people can share an address, a surname and a device and be unrelated.
Creating a relationship is not an identity merge.

A long-lived link is not an agreement. Where the relationship carries a term, an effective period, a renewal model or lapse semantics, it belongs to the continuing-relationship lifecycle and not here.
Direction is preserved where the relationship's semantics are directional.

nodes.detail: the next change is assessed against the new relationship

nodes.detail: a relationship change that alters an entitlement basis

nodes.headline: dependent rights and obligations recalculated; nothing else touched
nodes.detail: a further change recalculates from the new state

edges.label: Nothing depends on it
edges.when: the change is descriptive and nothing downstream reads it

edges.label: Entitlement unaffected

a relationship change that alters an entitlement basis

guardrails: A relationship change is not an identity change.
A relationship change is not an ownership transfer unless responsibility actually moves.
A structural relationship change is not a change to the commercial or contractual terms of a continuing relationship.
Historical relationship periods are preserved.
Actions queued under the superseded relationship do not execute.

identity.categoryTitle: Account structure, identity relationships & entity reconciliation

insufficientAlone: a subscription, contract, policy or membership reaching its end, which ends a term rather than a structural link

Record when it ended and why, appended to the relationship's history. The relationship having existed is not undone by its ending, and the period it covered stays readable - commitments made under it depended on it being real at the time

Were obligations created while the relationship was valid?
external:commitment-reconciliation
nodes.detail: a relationship ending with obligations created under it still live

nodes.headline: Must data or history be retained beyond the relationship?
Retain according to the applicable policy, marked as retained under an ended relationship rather than left looking like a live one

nodes.detail: a new relationship between the same entities is created on its own basis, and is a different relationship rather than a revival of this one

edges.label: Obligations outstanding

edges.label: Nothing outstanding
edges.when: the relationship carried only future behaviour
a relationship ending with obligations created under it still live

edges.when: policy or law requires the record to survive the relationship

edges.label: No retention requirement
edges.when: nothing beyond the relationship record itself has to be kept

distinctFrom.because: SUB-170 ends a term: a subscription, contract, policy or membership reaches cancellation, non-renewal, expiry, termination or lapse, and what stops is what the term was granting. This ends a structural link between two entities, and what stops is what depended on the link. An employee leaving an organisation ends the link and not the organisation's contract; a contract expiring ends the term and leaves the employee where they were.

guardrails: Ending a relationship does not delete the historical relationship.
Ending a relationship does not automatically cancel commitments created while it existed.
Unrelated relationships between the same entities remain unaffected.

Ending a structural link does not terminate an agreement that ran through it. A contract, subscription, policy or membership reaches its own end on its own terms, and inferring one from the other cancels things nobody cancelled.
governance.reusableRule: Ending a relationship removes future relationship-dependent behavior without erasing obligations legitimately created while the relationship existed.
governance.entityScope: the relationship that ended and the entities it connected
governance.entityNote: Only this relationship ends. Other relationships between the same two entities are untouched, and so is the record that this one existed. What ends here is a structural link. It does not own a term-bearing continuing agreement whose lifecycle includes effective dates, renewal, cancellation or lapse - an agreement that existed through this link reaches its own end on its own terms, in SUB-170.

identity.categoryTitle: Account structure, identity relationships & entity reconciliation

authority and capability delta applied; prior actions intact

edges.when: at least one capability is no longer carried, whether or not others were added
a role change that only adds capabilities

distinctFrom.because: A role change alters what someone may do. An identity attribute change alters who they are on record. Treating a role change as an identity change rebuilds the person and loses their history.

guardrails: A role change is not an identity change.
A role downgrade does not invalidate actions historically performed under the previous role.
Pending decisions are revalidated against current authority before the delta is applied.
The delta is scoped - capabilities common to both roles are left alone.
governance.reusableRule: Role changes should modify current authority through scoped deltas while preserving the history of actions validly performed under prior authority.
governance.entityScope: the person or member, the role, and the account or organisation the role is held in
governance.entityNote: A role belongs to a link between a person and an organisation. The same person holds different roles in different places, and changing one changes nothing about the others.

identity.categoryTitle: Account structure, identity relationships & entity reconciliation
identity.title: Parent state change → determine child impact → propagate selectively
identity.purpose: Let a parent's state reach only the children that genuinely depend on it, through a rule someone actually wrote.

requires: a material state change on a parent entity - an organisation suspended, a master account closed, a contract state changed, a parent resource disabled

nodes.headline: Parent state materially changed
Is a dependency model defined for this parent-child relationship?
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a parent state change with no defined dependency model

nodes.headline: Classify each child individually against the model: which are directly dependent on the parent's state, which are independently valid, and which carry open obligations. One verdict for the whole collection is the assumption that turns a suspended organisation into eleven deleted subsidiaries
How does each class resolve?
child state preserved; the parent change does not reach it
nodes.detail: a parent change that the model does make this child follow is evaluated when it happens. A parent going inactive does not delete a child that stands on its own

nodes.headline: Do the dependent children carry open obligations?
external:commitment-reconciliation
nodes.detail: propagation that would reach a child holding an open obligation

nodes.headline: Apply the defined consequence to the dependent children only, recording what propagated, to which children, and under which rule. Propagation that cannot say which rule produced it cannot be reviewed, reversed or explained
consequence applied to dependent children, scoped and recorded
nodes.detail: a further parent change is classified again against the model

edges.label: Defined
edges.when: a rule states which child states depend on which parent states, and how

edges.label: Not defined
edges.when: nothing states what this parent change should do to its children
a parent state change with no defined dependency model

edges.label: Directly dependent
edges.when: the model says this child's state follows the parent's

edges.label: Independently valid
edges.when: the child stands on its own basis and the model does not make it follow

edges.label: Obligations open
edges.when: a dependent child holds a commitment that would be destroyed by propagation

edges.label: Nothing open
edges.when: the dependent children hold nothing that outlives the propagation
propagation that would reach a child holding an open obligation

distinctFrom.because: This propagates downward through defined dependencies. REL-96 derives upward through an aggregation policy. They are opposite directions with different rules, and neither is the inverse of the other.

guardrails: A parent going inactive does not delete every child.
A parent restriction does not restrict every child globally unless the model defines it.
Propagation stays scoped and auditable - what went where, under which rule.
Where no dependency model exists, nothing propagates.
governance.reusableRule: Parent state changes should propagate only through explicitly defined dependencies rather than through assumed inheritance.
governance.entityScope: the parent whose state changed, and each child evaluated individually against the dependency model
governance.entityNote: Children are classified individually. A single verdict for the whole collection is the assumption this journey exists to prevent.

identity.categoryTitle: Account structure, identity relationships & entity reconciliation
identity.title: Child state change → recalculate aggregate parent state
identity.purpose: Derive a parent's state from its children through an explicit aggregation policy, recomputed from source rather than nudged by whichever child reported last.

requires: a change to a child state that the parent's aggregation policy reads
insufficientAlone: any child change, where no policy makes the parent depend on it

nodes.headline: Child state changed
Is an aggregation policy defined for this parent state?
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a child change with no aggregation policy to combine it

nodes.headline: Recompute the parent's derived state from the authoritative children using the defined policy, rather than adjusting it from the single child event that arrived. Recomputing from source means the aggregate can be rebuilt at any moment and cannot drift away from what the children actually say
Does the recomputed aggregate meet the parent's transition criteria?
Update the derived parent state, recording which children and which policy produced it, so the transition can be explained without recomputing it by hand
derived parent state updated from the aggregation policy
nodes.detail: the next relevant child change recomputes it again from source

nodes.headline: aggregate recomputed; parent state unchanged
nodes.detail: this is the ordinary outcome. One child changing is not the parent changing, and most child events correctly end here

edges.label: Defined
edges.when: a policy states how child states combine into the parent's, and what transitions it

edges.label: Not defined
edges.when: no policy states how these children combine
a child change with no aggregation policy to combine it

edges.label: Criteria met
edges.when: the policy's condition for moving the parent's state is satisfied

edges.label: Not met
edges.when: the aggregate moved and the parent's state does not

guardrails: One child's state does not automatically become the parent's state.
Aggregation semantics come from policy. ANY, ALL, majority and percentage thresholds are never inferred.
The aggregate is recomputable from the authoritative children rather than accumulated from events.
governance.reusableRule: Parent state derived from children must follow an explicit aggregation policy rather than simple state copying.
governance.entityScope: the parent and the full collection of children the policy reads
governance.entityNote: The aggregate is recomputed from the authoritative children, not incremented from the event that arrived. That is what keeps it rebuildable and stops it drifting.

identity.categoryTitle: Account structure, identity relationships & entity reconciliation
identity.title: Duplicate entity detected → assess → keep separate, link or merge
identity.purpose: Assess whether two records are the same entity, and route the answer - without consolidating anything.

requires: a match between records strong enough to be worth assessing
insufficientAlone: the same name
the same postcode or address
a similar spelling, which is what matching produces most of

nodes.headline: Potential duplicate detected

Collect the matching evidence and record its strength: verified identifiers, authoritative external IDs, declared ownership, verified contact points, business identifiers and relationship history. A match score is a reason to look and never a conclusion - the same email may be a shared family address, and the same phone number may be a workplace
What does the evidence actually support?
KEEP_SEPARATE; the records represent different entities
nodes.detail: stronger evidence later re-opens the assessment. Keeping two records apart is reversible; merging them usually is not, which is why this is the default when the evidence does not carry

nodes.headline: Entity link → shared context → preserve independent identity
nodes.detail: records that are related and genuinely distinct

nodes.headline: Identity or entity merge → reconcile → consolidate → verify
nodes.detail: a candidate set the evidence supports consolidating

nodes.headline: Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: an assessment the evidence cannot settle, or one whose consequences are too large to settle automatically

edges.label: Not the same entity
edges.when: the evidence is explained by something other than identity - a shared household, a shared workplace, a common name

edges.label: Related but distinct
edges.when: the records genuinely represent different entities that have a real relationship

edges.label: Same entity, consolidation looks safe
edges.when: verified identifiers or authoritative external IDs establish it, and nothing about the records makes merging risky

edges.label: Ambiguous or high-risk
edges.when: the evidence is suggestive and incomplete, or the records carry state that would be dangerous to consolidate wrongly
records that are related and genuinely distinct
a candidate set the evidence supports consolidating
an assessment the evidence cannot settle, or one whose consequences are too large to settle automatically

distinctFrom.because: Linking is one of the outcomes this assessment can reach. It is a separate journey because a link has its own semantics and its own sharing rules, which the assessment does not decide.

guardrails: The same name is not the same person.
A shared email or phone number may not prove the same entity - it depends on the model, and households and workplaces share both routinely.
Duplicate detection is not merge authorization. This journey assesses and routes; consolidating records is a separate mechanism with its own evidence requirements.
governance.reusableRule: Duplicate detection identifies a reconciliation candidate; merge requires separate evidence that consolidation is safe.
governance.entityScope: the candidate set of records suspected of representing one entity
governance.entityNote: The set is the unit. Three records suspected of being one person are assessed together, because a pairwise answer can be internally inconsistent.

identity.categoryTitle: Account structure, identity relationships & entity reconciliation
identity.title: Entity link → shared context → preserve independent identity
identity.purpose: Record that two entities are related and let defined context cross between them, while both remain two entities.

requires: a valid relationship or link between two distinct entities
insufficientAlone: a duplicate match, which is a question about whether they are one entity rather than evidence that they are two related ones

nodes.headline: Cross entity link established

Define what this link actually means - the same household, related accounts, linked profiles, a business relationship, a cross-product connection. The semantics decide what may be shared, and a link whose semantics are undefined shares nothing at all
What context do these link semantics explicitly permit sharing?
Share only the context the semantics explicitly permit. Anything not named is not shared, including things that would obviously be convenient

Confirm each entity keeps its own lifecycle state and history. Consent does not cross the link, and neither does entitlement or access, unless the relationship rules explicitly permit it - a household link is not permission to email everyone in the household
Is anything attempting to carry consent, entitlement, credentials or access across the link?
Block the propagation and record it. This is the specific failure a link becomes when it is quietly treated as a merge, and catching it here is cheaper than discovering it as a consent complaint
linked; two entities, two lifecycles, defined shared context
nodes.detail: the link's semantics may be changed, and the link may be ended, but neither turns it into a merge. Consolidating the records is a separate decision with separate evidence

edges.label: Defined shared context
edges.when: the link's semantics name specific context that may cross between the entities

edges.label: Nothing shared
edges.when: the link records a relationship and permits no context to cross - which is the common case

edges.label: Something is propagating
edges.when: a downstream process is treating the link as though the entities were one

edges.label: Nothing is
edges.when: only the permitted context crosses

guardrails: Linked is not merged.
Consent does not automatically propagate across linked identities.
Entitlement and access do not propagate unless the relationship rules explicitly permit it.
A link whose semantics are undefined shares nothing.
governance.reusableRule: Entity linking enables defined cross-entity context while preserving independent identity and lifecycle state.
governance.entityScope: the link itself, plus the two entities it connects
governance.entityNote: Each entity keeps its own lifecycle state and history. The link is a third record about them, not a step toward becoming one.

identity.categoryTitle: Account structure, identity relationships & entity reconciliation
identity.title: Entity split required → create separate records → allocate history and state safely
identity.purpose: Separate what should never have been one record, or what must now be managed apart, without copying the things that do not divide.

requires: an authoritative requirement to separate state currently held under one entity

nodes.headline: Entity split required
Determine the split basis - what actually distinguishes the resulting entities from one another. Without it, allocation becomes a series of individual guesses

Classify every piece of existing information as entity-specific, shared, ambiguous, historical or non-transferable. The last category is the one that gets missed: consent, entitlements, credentials and financial obligations do not divide by being copied, and duplicating one creates an obligation nobody incurred or a permission nobody gave
How does each classified item resolve?
Allocate the item to the entity it belongs to
Preserve the item through a relationship or reference model rather than duplicating it into both records. Two copies of one shared history diverge the first time either is edited
Leave it with the entity that holds it and record that it did not divide. A new record existing is not a reason for it to receive a copy of a consent, an entitlement or a debt
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: state that cannot be attributed to either resulting entity

nodes.headline: Recalculate each resulting entity's rights, permissions, entitlements, obligations and active journeys from what it now actually holds, rather than from what the source entity held

Record that the split occurred, when, and on what basis. History is not rewritten as though the records had always been separate - events that happened to the combined entity happened to the combined entity, and pretending otherwise makes every past event unattributable
entities separated; current state reconstructed, prior history preserved as it happened
nodes.detail: each resulting entity now has its own lifecycle. A further split is assessed against whichever of them requires it

edges.label: Clearly one entity's
edges.when: the item belongs unambiguously to one of the resulting entities

edges.label: Genuinely shared
edges.when: the item belongs to the relationship between them rather than to either

edges.label: Non-transferable
edges.when: consent, an entitlement, a credential or a financial obligation, none of which divides

edges.label: Ambiguous
edges.when: the item cannot be attributed on the split basis
state that cannot be attributed to either resulting entity

distinctFrom.because: A link connects two records that already exist separately. A split creates that separation where it did not exist, which means deciding what each side gets - and what neither side may simply be given a copy of.

guardrails: Consent, entitlements, credentials and financial obligations are never blindly duplicated across a split.
The audit trail preserves that a split occurred, when, and on what basis.
History is not rewritten as though the records had always been separate.
Ambiguous state is held unresolved rather than assigned by default.
governance.reusableRule: Entity splitting reconstructs independent current states while preserving the historical fact that the records were previously represented together.
governance.entityScope: the source entity and the entities that result from the split
governance.entityNote: The source entity's history remains the source entity's history. The resulting records inherit allocations, not a rewritten past.

identity.categoryTitle: Account structure, identity relationships & entity reconciliation
identity.title: Required relationship missing → orphan state → resolve or reassign
identity.purpose: Make a missing required relationship an explicit, findable state rather than a null field that active work quietly runs against.

requires: a relationship the entity requires to function being absent, invalid or removed - a work item without a required owner, a resource without a valid parent, a case without an account link, a dependent without a primary

nodes.headline: Required relationship missing

Record the entity as ORPHANED, naming which relationship is missing. This is an explicit state rather than a null field - null is unqueryable and unescalatable, and an entity with no owner has to be findable as an entity with no owner. Inherited deadlines and obligations keep running throughout; being orphaned is our problem and does not pause what was already owed
Is there a deterministic replacement relationship?
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: an orphan with several possible replacements and no rule between them

nodes.headline: Is there a safe temporary holding scope for this entity?
Hold the entity in the explicit unresolved queue, with its inherited deadlines and obligations intact and visible. Held is a state someone can query and escalate; a null relationship is neither
until a valid relationship is restored or established
nodes.detail: timeout after the resolution SLA for this entity type

nodes.headline: Establish the replacement relationship, preserving the entity's inherited deadlines and obligations exactly as they stood. Reassignment changes who is connected, never what is owed or by when

Revalidate the entity's current state against the restored relationship before resuming. The relationship changed, so what the entity is entitled to or responsible for under the new one may differ from what it held under the old
relationship restored; entity revalidated and resumed
nodes.detail: a further missing relationship opens its own orphan state

nodes.headline: The resolution SLA passed with the entity still orphaned - what does policy do?
Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: an orphaned entity that could not be reconnected

nodes.headline: orphaned entity handled under its policy end state
nodes.detail: a valid relationship becoming available later re-opens this; the entity was never silently discarded

edges.label: Exactly one valid replacement
edges.when: the rules resolve to a single valid counterpart

edges.label: Several possible
edges.when: more than one counterpart could be valid and nothing decides between them

edges.label: None available
edges.when: no valid counterpart currently exists
an orphan with several possible replacements and no rule between them

edges.label: Holding scope exists
edges.when: an explicit unresolved queue or state can hold it without work proceeding against a missing relationship

edges.label: None
edges.when: nothing can safely hold it while active work continues against it

edges.label: on event
edges.when: a valid relationship is restored or established

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: an orphan is carrying live obligations with nobody attached to them, so an unresolved one escalates rather than waiting quietly

edges.label: Escalate
edges.when: the entity carries obligations that make an owner necessary rather than desirable

edges.label: Terminal handling
edges.when: policy defines an end state for entities that cannot be reconnected
an orphaned entity that could not be reconnected

distinctFrom.because: OWN-51 routes work that has never had an owner. This handles an entity that had a required relationship and lost it, which means inherited deadlines and obligations are already running against it.

guardrails: A missing relationship never silently becomes a null field while active work continues.
A parent or owner is not guessed from weak evidence. Several candidates route to a person.
Inherited deadlines and obligations stay intact while the entity is orphaned.
governance.reusableRule: When a required relationship disappears, the entity should enter an explicit unresolved state until a valid relationship is restored.
governance.entityScope: the entity missing its required relationship, and the relationship type that is absent
governance.entityNote: One orphan state per missing relationship. An entity missing two required links is in two unresolved states, each resolvable independently.

identity.title: Post-completion issue → validate → remedy route
identity.purpose: Establish whether something delivered has left an obligation unresolved, and which recovery mechanism could satisfy it.

requires: a concrete problem with a completed fulfillment or service: a wrong item or result, damaged output, a missing component, a quality problem, a service defect, an incorrect configuration or an incomplete outcome
insufficientAlone: negative feedback about the experience, which reports a feeling rather than naming a problem with what was delivered
a low satisfaction score

nodes.headline: Post completion issue reported
Capture the issue id, the fulfillment or service it concerns, the problem as reported, the affected scope, when it was reported and whatever evidence exists
Does an existing recovery case already cover this problem?

Attach the new evidence and context to the existing case. No second recovery lifecycle is opened - two remedies running against one obligation produce two replacements or two refunds, and the second is found by accounting rather than by the process that issued it
attached to the existing recovery case
nodes.detail: if that case closes with the problem still present, the recurrence is assessed on its own terms rather than as a fresh report

nodes.headline: Establish whether the report describes an unresolved obligation a remedy could satisfy, or an experience that fell short without anything having gone wrong. Both are real; only the first creates something to fix
Is there an actionable unresolved obligation?
Acknowledge and explain, closing according to policy. No defect is manufactured to give the report somewhere to go, and no refund is issued as a way of ending the conversation
heard; no unresolved obligation and no remedy owed
nodes.detail: new evidence of an actual defect re-opens this. Repetition of the same report is itself worth reading, without becoming a defect by repetition

nodes.headline: Classify the remedy route the problem actually implies - a correction, a reperformance, a replacement, a return, a refund review, a service recovery, or another policy-defined remedy. Refund is one route among several rather than the default, and choosing it because it is the easiest to execute leaves the customer without the thing they wanted
Remedy selection → resolve obligation → financial handoff if needed
nodes.detail: a confirmed unresolved obligation needing a remedy decision

edges.label: Already covered
edges.when: an open case concerns the same defect on the same obligation

edges.label: Nothing open
edges.when: no existing case covers it

edges.label: Actionable
edges.when: something identifiable was owed and is not what was delivered

edges.label: Not actionable
edges.when: the delivery matched what was owed and the experience still disappointed
a confirmed unresolved obligation needing a remedy decision

distinctFrom.because: FBK-44 starts from someone's account of an experience and asks whether any operational issue exists. This starts from a concrete problem with something already delivered and asks which recovery route would fix it - the obligation is known to exist and the question is what satisfies it.

guardrails: An issue reported is not a confirmed defect.
Negative feedback alone does not establish remedy eligibility.
Not every issue defaults to a refund.
An existing case covering the same obligation suppresses a second recovery lifecycle.
governance.reusableRule: Post-completion problems should first establish the unresolved obligation before selecting the remedy intended to satisfy it.
governance.entityScope: the completed fulfillment or service, and the specific problem reported against it
governance.entityNote: The issue is scoped to the fulfillment it concerns. A second problem with the same order is a second issue unless it is the same defect described again.

identity.title: Return request → eligibility → authorize, reject or review
identity.purpose: Decide whether something may enter a return process, as a decision separate from whether money is owed.

requires: a request to send back an identified item, resource or deliverable
insufficientAlone: an expression of dissatisfaction, which is a report rather than a request to return anything

nodes.headline: Return requested
Capture the request id, the item or resource, the quantity or scope, the reason, the requester and the request time
Does a return process apply to this at all?
Remedy selection → resolve obligation → financial handoff if needed
nodes.detail: a return requested against something that cannot be returned

nodes.headline: Is a return eligibility policy defined for this?
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a return request with no governing eligibility policy

nodes.headline: What does the policy determine?
Record RETURN_REJECTED with the reason drawn from the policy that ruled it out
RETURN_REJECTED; the original fulfillment is unchanged
nodes.detail: a return refused does not settle whether another remedy is owed - that question is separate and is asked separately

nodes.headline: Record RETURN_UNDER_REVIEW and gather what the decision requires. Nothing is authorised while it is under review
until a decision is recorded
nodes.detail: timeout after the decision SLA

nodes.headline: What was decided?
Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: a return decision outliving its SLA

nodes.headline: Record RETURN_AUTHORIZED with the scope, the method and the validity. Authorising a return permits the resource to come back and decides nothing about whether money is owed - refund eligibility is a separate question with its own rules and its own answer
Return authorized → in transit, received, lost or expired
nodes.detail: an authorised return

edges.label: Returnable
edges.when: the thing exists physically or as a revocable deliverable and can be sent back

edges.label: Nothing to return
edges.when: the delivery was a service performed, a consumed resource, or something with no return path
a return requested against something that cannot be returned

edges.label: Defined
edges.when: policy states what may be returned, within what window and on what conditions

edges.label: Not defined
edges.when: no policy covers returns of this kind
a return request with no governing eligibility policy

edges.label: Eligible
edges.when: the policy's conditions are met deterministically

edges.label: Ineligible
edges.when: the policy rules it out deterministically

edges.label: Requires review or evidence
edges.when: the policy leaves this case to a decision rather than a rule

edges.label: on event
edges.when: a decision is recorded

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a return request left undecided leaves someone holding something they were told they might send back, with no way to know whether they may

edges.label: Authorized
edges.when: the reviewer permitted the return

edges.label: Rejected
edges.when: the reviewer refused it
a return decision outliving its SLA
an authorised return

distinctFrom.because: This grants permission for a resource to come back. REM-153 tracks whether it actually does, which fails independently and often.

guardrails: A return requested is not a return authorized.
Return eligibility rules are never invented.
Refund eligibility and return eligibility may be different decisions with different answers.
governance.reusableRule: A return request creates a decision about whether the original fulfillment may enter a return process; it does not itself reverse the fulfillment.
governance.entityScope: the return request and the original fulfillment it concerns
governance.entityNote: Return eligibility and refund eligibility are different questions with different rules. Authorising a return decides only the first.

identity.title: Return authorized → in transit, received, lost or expired
identity.purpose: Track whether an authorised return actually comes back, and hold the states where it might not have.

requires: an active return authorisation with a scope and a validity

nodes.headline: Return authorization active

Define the return method, the destination, the scope and quantity, the authorisation's validity and the tracking reference where one exists. Record AUTHORIZED - permission to return, with nothing yet moved
until the return is dispatched by the requester, or the return is received by us, or a return exception is reported
nodes.detail: timeout after the authorisation's validity

nodes.headline: What happened?

Record IN_RETURN_TRANSIT. A carrier accepting the parcel is not the resource having returned to us - a return-dependent remedy waits for receipt, and issuing one on a tracking number means issuing it for something that may never arrive
until the return is received, or a transit exception is reported
nodes.detail: timeout after the expected transit window plus its tolerance

nodes.headline: Which arrived first?

Record RETURN_UNKNOWN and suppress any return-dependent outcome. A return we cannot locate is neither one that arrived nor one that was never sent, and acting as though it were either produces a remedy issued against nothing or a customer refused for something they did send
Record LOST or EXCEPTION with what the carrier reported, and who bears the risk under the return method that was used
external:external-status-reconciliation
nodes.detail: a return whose whereabouts or outcome could not be established

nodes.headline: Record EXPIRED_UNUSED - the authorisation lapsed and nothing came back. Whether another remedy remains available is a separate question and is asked separately
EXPIRED_UNUSED; nothing returned and the authorisation has lapsed
nodes.detail: a fresh return request is assessed on its own eligibility. The original obligation, if still unresolved, remains so

nodes.headline: Returned item or deliverable → inspect → accept, reject or partial
nodes.detail: a returned resource arriving

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the return is dispatched by the requester, the return is received by us, a return exception is reported

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: an authorisation that lapses unused releases whatever was being held against it, and the customer keeps the thing rather than being left in an open process

edges.label: Dispatched
edges.when: the requester handed it to a carrier or return channel

edges.label: Received
edges.when: it arrived with us

edges.label: Exception
edges.when: the carrier or channel reports it lost, damaged in transit or undeliverable

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the return is received, a transit exception is reported

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a return that has neither arrived nor been reported lost is unknown, and treating our silence as its loss writes off something that may be two days away

edges.label: The return
edges.when: the resource reached us

edges.label: An exception
edges.when: the carrier reported a problem
a return whose whereabouts or outcome could not be established
a returned resource arriving

guardrails: Authorized is not returned.
Carrier acceptance is not the resource having returned to the business.
No return-dependent outcome is issued from a tracking number alone unless policy explicitly permits it.
governance.reusableRule: Return authorization establishes permission to return; the return remains operationally unresolved until the resource's return outcome is known.
governance.entityScope: the authorised return and the resource travelling under it
governance.entityNote: A carrier accepting the parcel is a fact about the carrier. The return-dependent remedy waits for receipt by us, not for a tracking number existing.

identity.title: Returned item or deliverable → inspect → accept, reject or partial
identity.purpose: Judge what came back against the conditions it was authorised under, keeping receipt and acceptance apart.

requires: a returned resource physically or logically received against an authorisation

nodes.headline: Returned resource received

Record that the resource was received, with what actually arrived. This fact stands whatever the inspection concludes - a rejected return is still something we are holding, and losing track of it because it failed inspection is how goods disappear into a warehouse nobody reconciles
Are the inspection criteria defined for this kind of return?
Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a returned resource with no defined acceptance criteria

nodes.headline: Inspect against the criteria that apply - identity, quantity, condition, completeness, included components, the authorised scope, and integrity where it matters
What did the inspection find?
Record RETURN_ACCEPTED for the full authorised scope
Record PARTIALLY_ACCEPTED, naming exactly which scope is accepted and which is not. The two are carried separately because whatever remedy follows applies to one of them and not the other
Record RETURN_REJECTED_AFTER_RECEIPT with the reason. The receipt record stands - we still physically hold the thing, and what happens to it is part of what the remedy decision now has to cover
Remedy selection → resolve obligation → financial handoff if needed
nodes.detail: a return inspected and its accepted scope established

edges.label: Defined
edges.when: policy states what condition, completeness and scope the return has to meet

edges.label: Not defined
edges.when: no policy states what an acceptable return looks like here
a returned resource with no defined acceptance criteria

edges.label: Fully acceptable
edges.when: everything authorised arrived and meets the conditions

edges.label: Partially acceptable
edges.when: some of the returned scope meets the conditions and some does not

edges.label: Not acceptable
edges.when: what arrived does not meet the conditions it was authorised under
a return inspected and its accepted scope established

guardrails: Received is not accepted.
Inspection criteria are policy-defined rather than judged case by case.
A rejected return does not erase the fact that the resource was physically received.
Partial outcomes preserve the exact accepted and rejected scope.
governance.reusableRule: A returned resource satisfies the return requirement only after the received scope has been evaluated against the applicable acceptance rules.
governance.entityScope: the returned resource as received, and the return case it arrived under
governance.entityNote: Physical receipt is recorded regardless of the inspection's outcome. A rejected return is still an object we are holding.

identity.title: Replacement decision → allocate → fulfill → confirm
identity.purpose: Deliver a second time against the same promise, tied to the defect it exists to resolve.

requires: a replacement authorised as the remedy for an identified defect

nodes.headline: Replacement remedy authorized

Record the replacement's relationship to the original fulfillment and the specific defect it exists to resolve. The original's history stays intact - a replacement is a second fulfillment against the same obligation, not a correction of the first one's record
Determine the replacement scope - which part of the original is being replaced, which is not, and whether what is being sent is identical or an accepted equivalent
Is a replacement resource available?
Does policy permit waiting for availability?
until a replacement resource becomes available
nodes.detail: timeout after the tolerable wait for this remedy

nodes.headline: Create the replacement fulfillment without a new commercial charge, unless policy explicitly requires one. A remedy that bills again for what was already paid for is not a remedy, and it converts a recoverable problem into a dispute
until the replacement is fulfilled and delivered, or the replacement fails or is cancelled
nodes.detail: timeout after the remedy deadline

nodes.headline: What happened to the replacement?
Remedy execution → verify outcome → close or continue recovery
nodes.detail: a replacement delivered

nodes.headline: Remedy selection → resolve obligation → financial handoff if needed
nodes.detail: a replacement that cannot be delivered

edges.label: Available

a low survey score with no incident behind it

Establish what failed, what it cost the customer, whether it has been resolved, whether they are still affected, and whether some other process is already handling it
Is another recovery process already handling this failure?
deferred to the process already handling it
nodes.detail: if that process closes with the customer still affected, this re-opens - two apologies from two systems is worse than one, because it proves neither knew about the other

nodes.headline: Is the underlying issue still unresolved?
external:operational-resolution
nodes.detail: a failure that is still ongoing

nodes.headline: Is a recovery communication actually useful here?
resolved without contact
nodes.detail: a recurrence, or any sign they did notice, re-opens this

nodes.headline: Does policy and the actual impact support compensation?
Compensation decision → eligibility → grant or reject → deliver
nodes.detail: a remedy that policy and impact both support

nodes.headline: Say what failed, what was done about it, and what stops it happening again. No discount standing in for an explanation - a remedy offered instead of an account of what went wrong reads as buying silence
failure acknowledged, no remedy owed
nodes.detail: a recurrence changes the assessment, and repetition is itself part of the impact

edges.label: Already handled
edges.when: an open case, an assigned owner or another recovery journey covers the same incident

edges.label: Nobody on it
edges.when: no existing process covers it

edges.label: Still broken
edges.when: the customer remains affected

edges.label: Resolved
edges.when: the failure is over and the customer is no longer affected
a failure that is still ongoing

edges.label: Useful
edges.when: the customer noticed, or would want to know it was handled

edges.label: Not useful
edges.when: the failure was resolved before it reached them - raising it now creates the concern it would be apologising for

edges.label: Owed
edges.when: the impact and the policy both support a remedy

edges.label: Not owed
edges.when: the failure was real but no remedy is justified - which is most failures
a remedy that policy and impact both support

guardrails: Negative feedback is not a confirmed service failure. One is a report of an experience, the other is a record of something going wrong.
A discount is not a default apology. Compensation follows impact and policy, not the awkwardness of the conversation.
An existing support case suppresses this entirely. A parallel recovery journey contradicts the person already handling it.
governance.reusableRule: Service recovery should reflect the actual failure, current resolution state and justified remedy rather than use compensation as a default response.
governance.entityScope: person or account plus the experience or service entity that failed
governance.entityNote: The recovery belongs to the failure. A second unrelated failure is a second instance, and one apology does not cover both.

identity.title: Recovery signal → observation buffer → stable or relapse
identity.purpose: Keep the distance between a good sign and an actual recovery, so a relapse is still being watched for when it happens.

requires: a positive behaviour in a context that had deteriorated or received a recovery intervention
insufficientAlone: a single login
a single payment attempt, which is an attempt rather than a restored payment relationship
an opened or clicked message

nodes.headline: Positive signal after deterioration
