nodes.headline: Apply the transition idempotently, keyed so that a redelivery of the same job cannot apply it twice
scheduled transition applied against a validated current state
nodes.detail: a further scheduled change is its own intention with its own validation

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the schedule is cancelled, the schedule is replaced by a newer one

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: reaching the effective time is the ordinary path; the wait is watching for the schedule being withdrawn before it gets there

edges.label: Matches
edges.when: the current version is the one the transition was written against

edges.label: Superseded
edges.when: a newer authoritative change has already moved the entity past this

edges.label: Assumptions changed
edges.when: the entity still exists in a comparable state but the reasoning behind the schedule no longer holds
a schedule whose underlying assumptions no longer hold

edges.label: Already applied
edges.when: a previous delivery of this same job already made the change

edges.label: Not yet applied
edges.when: the transition has not run

distinctFrom.because: An expiry is one specific scheduled transition with entity-specific consequences. This is the general mechanism, and every other scheduled change - a plan change at period end, a future cancellation, a scheduled restriction - runs through it.

guardrails: Every scheduled action validates at execution time rather than trusting the state it was written against.
An old scheduled transition never overwrites a newer authoritative change.
Cancelling or replacing a schedule invalidates the original job rather than leaving both alive.
Duplicate execution applies the transition once. Redelivery is expected, not exceptional.
governance.reusableRule: Future transitions are intentions, not guaranteed outcomes; their validity must be rechecked when execution time arrives.
governance.entityScope: the scheduled transition plus the target entity and the version it expected to find
governance.entityNote: The expected version is the mechanism. Without it, execution has no way to tell whether the world moved underneath the schedule.

identity.categoryTitle: Entity merge, account closure, data lifecycle & terminal states
identity.title: Identity or entity merge → reconcile → consolidate → verify
identity.purpose: Consolidate records that represent one entity, after every dependent state has been reconciled under its own authority rule.

requires: an explicit merge authorization following a duplicate assessment, naming the sources, the target and the authority that authorised it
insufficientAlone: a duplicate detection, which produces a candidate rather than a decision
a high match score
an assessment concluding the records are probably the same, without an authorisation to act on it

nodes.headline: Merge explicitly authorized

Create the auditable merge operation: source entity IDs, the canonical target, the basis, the authority that authorised it, the time, and every conflict decision as it is made. Provenance is what makes the result reviewable - without it the consolidated record cannot say where any part of itself came from

Inventory the dependent state before anything is touched: identity attributes, consent, preferences, contact points, entitlements, purchases, subscriptions, support cases, opportunities, credentials, active journeys, open obligations and relationships. Each of these answers to a different authority, and a merge that reads them as one list applies one rule to all of them
Is this merge reversible?
Does the evidence and authority meet the higher bar an irreversible merge requires?
not merged; evidence sized for a reversible operation
nodes.detail: stronger evidence, or an architecture that makes the merge reversible, re-opens this. Leaving two records separate is recoverable and this is not

nodes.headline: Does conflicting state exist across the sources?
Merge conflict → safe state → resolve → continue or abort
nodes.detail: conflicting state discovered during merge

nodes.headline: Consolidate each state type under its own authority rule. There is no newest-value-wins applied across the board: a newer contact point may supersede an older one, a newer consent does not supersede an older withdrawal, an entitlement is reconciled rather than either kept or duplicated, and a financial obligation is never added to itself
Repoint dependent relationships and active processes onto the canonical entity, so nothing continues to run against a representation that has been superseded

Invalidate the actions still queued against the superseded representations. A downstream synchronisation running on its own schedule will otherwise restore what was just consolidated, which undoes the merge while reporting success

Verify the merge did what it was for and nothing more: no critical obligation lost, no permission more permissive than any source held, no entitlement duplicated, no duplicate active journey still running, and the source history still traceable
Did verification pass?
merged into the canonical entity, with provenance and source history intact
nodes.detail: a further duplicate candidate involving this entity is assessed on its own evidence, with this merge in the record

edges.label: Reversible
edges.when: the architecture can separate the records again if the decision turns out to be wrong

edges.label: Irreversible
edges.when: consolidation cannot be undone once applied

edges.label: Sufficient
edges.when: verified identifiers or authoritative external IDs establish it, at the standard an unrecoverable decision demands

edges.label: Not sufficient
edges.when: the evidence would justify a reversible merge and not this one

edges.label: Conflicts present
edges.when: two sources hold incompatible values for state that matters

edges.label: No conflicts
edges.when: every state type reconciles without contradiction
conflicting state discovered during merge

edges.label: Passed
edges.when: every check holds

edges.label: Failed
edges.when: a check found a lost obligation, a widened permission, a duplicated entitlement or a surviving duplicate journey

distinctFrom.because: Account consolidation unifies business structure and leaves the people distinct. This consolidates the representations of one entity, which is a decision about identity and carries a far higher evidence bar.

guardrails: A merge never duplicates a financial obligation.
An opt-out never disappears because another profile was opted in.
Provenance is preserved - the consolidated record can say where each part of it came from.
An irreversible merge requires stronger evidence and authority than a reversible one.
governance.reusableRule: Entity merge consolidates representations only after dependent state has been reconciled according to the authority rules of each state type.
governance.entityScope: the source entities, the canonical target, and the merge operation itself as an auditable record
governance.entityNote: The merge operation is its own entity. Its record of conflict decisions and provenance is what makes the consolidated result reviewable, and often what makes it reversible.

identity.categoryTitle: Entity merge, account closure, data lifecycle & terminal states
identity.title: Merge conflict → safe state → resolve → continue or abort
identity.purpose: Fail safe wherever consolidating would require inventing an authority the system does not have.

requires: state that two sources hold incompatibly: contradictory identity attributes, a permission conflict, different ownership claims, incompatible account states, duplicate active obligations, or a credential or security conflict

nodes.headline: Critical merge conflict detected
Classify the conflict by domain. The domain decides which authority rule applies, and there is no rule that applies across identity, permission, ownership, obligation and credentials at once
Does a deterministic authority rule exist for this domain?

Apply the rule and record the basis. A conflict resolved in order to make the merge succeed is not resolved - it has been decided by the only party with an interest in the answer, which is whoever wanted the merge

Record the affected state as MERGE_CONFLICT. The most permissive consent or access value is never selected by default - defaulting that way resolves every ambiguity in the direction that cannot be undone, and it is the direction a merge is already biased toward
Is this an ambiguous identity conflict?
Can the merge safely continue on the portions that carry no conflict?
Hold the entire merge. Where identity itself is in doubt, consolidating anything assumes the thing the merge was supposed to establish
Consolidate only the portions carrying no conflict and no dependency on conflicted state, leaving the rest explicitly unmerged rather than quietly merged with a chosen value
until an authoritative or manual resolution is recorded, or the merge is aborted
nodes.detail: timeout after the conflict resolution SLA

nodes.headline: Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: a merge conflict outliving its resolution SLA

nodes.headline: How was it settled?
RESOLVED; the merge may complete
nodes.detail: a further conflict in the same merge opens its own instance

nodes.headline: Abort the merge, unwinding whatever was partially consolidated where that is possible, and recording precisely what could not be unwound. The sources remain separate and the attempt remains in the record
ABORTED; sources remain separate
nodes.detail: a new merge requires new evidence. That an earlier attempt was aborted is part of what the next one is judged against

nodes.headline: PARTIALLY_RECONCILED; conflicted state left separate and marked
nodes.detail: what remains unmerged is named rather than left as a vague inconsistency, so it can be resolved later on its own evidence

edges.label: Rule exists
edges.when: policy states which source wins for this kind of state, and why

edges.label: No rule
edges.when: nothing states how this conflict resolves

edges.label: Identity itself is in doubt
edges.when: the conflict suggests these may not be one entity at all

edges.label: Identity is established
edges.when: the conflict is about state held by an entity we are confident is one

edges.label: Independent portions exist
edges.when: some state can be consolidated without depending on anything in conflict

edges.label: Everything is entangled
edges.when: the conflicted state is load-bearing for the rest

edges.label: on event
edges.when: an authoritative or manual resolution is recorded, the merge is aborted

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a merge held in conflict leaves two records in a half-consolidated state, which is worse than either outcome and worth escalating rather than waiting out
a merge conflict outliving its resolution SLA

edges.label: Resolved
edges.when: an authority determined the answer and the merge may complete

edges.label: Aborted
edges.when: the merge should not proceed

edges.label: Partially reconciled, remainder unresolvable
edges.when: the independent portions consolidated and the conflicted state stays separate

guardrails: A conflict is never resolved merely to make the merge succeed.
The most permissive consent or access state is never chosen by default.
An ambiguous identity conflict stops the entire merge rather than part of it.
What could not be unwound after an abort is recorded rather than assumed away.
governance.reusableRule: Merge conflicts should fail safe whenever consolidation would require inventing authority that the system does not possess.
governance.entityScope: the merge operation and the specific state in conflict
governance.entityNote: The conflict attaches to particular state, not to the whole merge. Some conflicts stop everything and most do not, and telling them apart is the journey's main work.

identity.categoryTitle: Entity merge, account closure, data lifecycle & terminal states
identity.title: Account consolidation → dependency reconciliation → unified relationship
identity.purpose: Unify business structure across accounts while every person involved stays a separate person.

requires: an authorized consolidation naming the accounts and the canonical target
insufficientAlone: two accounts sharing a domain, a billing address or an administrator

nodes.headline: Account consolidation authorized
Determine the canonical account structure - which account survives and what the consolidated shape actually is
Inventory across every account being consolidated: members, roles, contracts, subscriptions, resources, entitlements, billing relationships, open cases, ownership and active obligations
Does any part of this require treating two people as one?
consolidation stopped; it requires an identity merge
nodes.detail: consolidating two people into one identity is a different decision with a far higher evidence bar, assessed and authorised separately. A consolidation that needs it has exceeded what it was authorised to do

nodes.headline: Are the resources transferable to the canonical account?
Transfer the resources according to policy, keeping their history with them
Retain the resource under its original relationship, referenced from the canonical account rather than moved into it. A reference keeps it reachable without pretending it changed hands
Do the accounts carry conflicting obligations?
external:commitment-reconciliation
nodes.detail: obligations that cannot both survive the consolidated structure

nodes.headline: Recalculate account-level roles, access, entitlements, routing and aggregate states from what the consolidated account actually holds. Permissions are recalculated rather than unioned - a union grants everyone the highest access anyone previously had, which turns a structural tidy-up into privilege escalation
Verify that no entitlement was duplicated, no obligation lost, no access became broader than any source account granted, and no resource left orphaned
Did verification pass?
accounts consolidated; identities untouched
nodes.detail: a further consolidation is assessed against the canonical structure this produced

nodes.headline: Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: a consolidation whose verification failed

edges.label: It does
edges.when: the consolidation only works if two member records are the same person

edges.label: It does not
edges.when: every member remains a distinct identity in the consolidated structure

edges.label: Transferable
edges.when: policy and the resource itself allow it to move

edges.label: Not transferable
edges.when: a contract, a licence or the resource's own nature keeps it where it is

edges.label: Conflicting
edges.when: two accounts hold obligations that cannot both stand in one structure

edges.label: Compatible
edges.when: the obligations coexist in the consolidated structure
obligations that cannot both survive the consolidated structure

edges.label: Passed
edges.when: every check holds

edges.label: Failed
edges.when: a duplicated entitlement, a lost obligation, widened access or an orphaned resource was found
a consolidation whose verification failed

guardrails: Account consolidation is not person identity merge.
Members of consolidated accounts do not become the same identity.
Account-level permissions are recalculated rather than unioned.
A resource that cannot transfer is referenced rather than moved.
governance.reusableRule: Account consolidation unifies business structure while preserving independent identities and reconciling account-level obligations explicitly.
governance.entityScope: the accounts being consolidated and the canonical structure that results
governance.entityNote: Accounts consolidate; people do not. The members of the consolidated account remain distinct identities with distinct consent and distinct history.

identity.categoryTitle: Entity merge, account closure, data lifecycle & terminal states
identity.title: Primary relationship transfer → validate new primary → transfer dependencies
identity.purpose: Move a dependent entity to a new primary, carrying only what the primary relationship actually governs.

requires: an authorized transfer naming the dependent entity, the outgoing primary and the incoming one

nodes.headline: Primary relationship transfer authorized
Is the proposed new primary relationship valid?
transfer rejected; the existing primary relationship stands
nodes.detail: a different incoming primary is validated on its own terms. The dependent is never left between two primaries while the question is open

nodes.headline: Identify what the primary relationship actually governs: rights, notifications, responsibilities, billing, access, ownership and open obligations. Anything the dependent holds on its own basis is deliberately not on this list

Transfer only the dependencies the primary relationship governs, preserving the historical primary relationship and the period it covered. Existing obligations move with their deadlines unchanged rather than disappearing in the handover
Does the dependent hold permission or consent on its own basis?
Preserve it independently. It does not transfer, and the incoming primary's state is not inherited over it - a dependent who opted out does not become opted in because their primary is
Verify the dependent now holds exactly one valid required primary relationship - not zero, and not two
Did verification pass?
primary relationship transferred; independent state preserved
nodes.detail: a further transfer is validated against the current primary

nodes.headline: Required relationship missing → orphan state → resolve or reassign
nodes.detail: a dependent left without exactly one valid required primary

edges.label: Valid
edges.when: the incoming primary can hold this relationship and is entitled to

edges.label: Not valid
edges.when: the incoming primary is ineligible, or the relationship is not permitted between these types

edges.label: It does
edges.when: the dependent gave or withheld something itself, rather than inheriting it

edges.label: It does not
edges.when: everything it held came through the primary relationship

edges.label: Exactly one valid primary
edges.when: the transfer landed cleanly

edges.label: None, or more than one
edges.when: the dependent is left without a required primary, or holding two
a dependent left without exactly one valid required primary

distinctFrom.because: Changing which primary a dependent hangs from moves a relationship. It consolidates nothing and neither party's identity changes.

guardrails: A primary relationship transfer is not an identity merge.
The historical primary relationship and its period are preserved.
Existing obligations do not disappear during a transfer, and their deadlines do not reset.
The dependent's own permission and consent are never overwritten by the incoming primary's.
governance.reusableRule: Changing a primary relationship transfers only the dependencies governed by that relationship, not every state associated with either party.
governance.entityScope: the dependent entity, its outgoing primary and its incoming one
governance.entityNote: The dependent's own permissions and consent are not part of the transfer. They belong to the dependent and stay with it.

identity.categoryTitle: Entity merge, account closure, data lifecycle & terminal states
identity.title: Role or responsibility handover → effective-time transfer → continue
identity.purpose: Move a role between two people at a defined moment, without changing anything before it or rewriting anything behind it.

requires: an authorized handover naming the outgoing actor, the incoming actor, the scope and the effective time

nodes.headline: Responsibility handover authorized

Define the outgoing actor, the incoming actor, the scope, the effective time and the reason. A handover scheduled for a future date is not an authority change now - until the effective time the outgoing actor still holds the role and everything in it
Inventory what travels with the role: open work, deadlines, approvals, scheduled actions, commitments and the context needed to continue any of them
Is the incoming actor eligible and authorized for this role?
Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: a handover into an actor who cannot hold the role

nodes.headline: Prepare the transfer without activating it. Nothing about the outgoing actor's authority changes yet, and nothing about the incoming actor's does either
until the handover is cancelled, or the handover is superseded by another
nodes.detail: timeout after the effective time

nodes.headline: handover cancelled or superseded before its effective time
nodes.detail: the outgoing actor retained the role throughout, so nothing has to be undone - which is the point of not moving authority at the moment of authorisation

nodes.headline: At the effective time, revalidate both actors and the target entity. Weeks can pass between authorising a handover and it taking effect, and either actor may have left, changed role or lost the authority the handover assumed
Are both actors and the target still valid at the effective time?
Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: a handover whose assumptions did not survive to its effective time

nodes.headline: Activate the new responsibility from the effective time, with the inherited deadlines and obligations exactly as they stood. The handover changes who is answerable, never what is owed or by when

Invalidate the outgoing actor's future scheduled actions where their authority has now ended. Decisions they made while holding the role remain historical facts and are not touched - what changes is what they may do next
responsibility handed over at its effective time
nodes.detail: a further handover is scheduled and validated on its own terms

edges.label: Eligible
edges.when: they hold the authority the role requires and nothing disqualifies them

edges.label: Not eligible
edges.when: they cannot hold the role, or their authority does not cover its scope
a handover into an actor who cannot hold the role

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the handover is cancelled, the handover is superseded by another

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: reaching the effective moment is the ordinary path; the wait watches for the handover being withdrawn before it gets there

edges.label: Still valid
edges.when: nothing that the handover assumed has changed

edges.label: Something moved
edges.when: an actor has left, lost authority, or the target no longer exists as scoped
a handover whose assumptions did not survive to its effective time

distinctFrom.because: OWN-54 moves ownership of one work item now. This moves a role and everything it carries at a future effective point, which is why both actors are revalidated when that point arrives rather than when it was scheduled.
REL-94 changes one person's role. This moves a role from one person to another, which means two actors to validate and a set of open work that has to travel intact.

guardrails: A future handover is not an immediate authority change.
Historical decisions by the outgoing actor remain historical facts.
Inherited deadlines do not reset at the handover.
Both actors are revalidated at the effective time, not at the time of authorisation.
governance.reusableRule: Responsibility handover changes future authority at a defined effective point while preserving the history and obligations of the role.
governance.entityScope: the role or responsibility, its outgoing holder and its incoming one
governance.entityNote: A handover has an effective time, and that time is load-bearing. Authorising it today does not move authority today.

identity.categoryTitle: Entity merge, account closure, data lifecycle & terminal states
identity.title: Account closure request → validate → resolve blockers → close
identity.purpose: End an account relationship once the obligations that legitimately block it are resolved, and end nothing else.

requires: a closure request against an identified account
insufficientAlone: a cancelled subscription, which ends a commercial relationship rather than the account
a data deletion request, which is a different lifecycle with a different authority
a long period of inactivity

nodes.headline: Account closure requested
Record CLOSURE_REQUESTED, and determine who requested it, whether they hold the authority to, the account's current state, its open blockers and its dependent relationships
Does the requester hold authority to close this account?
closure not requested by an authorised party; account unchanged
nodes.detail: a request from an authorised party is assessed on its own terms

nodes.headline: Is closure permitted now?
Surface the exact blocker. Telling someone they cannot close their account without saying why produces a support case rather than a closure, and it reads as an obstacle rather than a requirement
until the surfaced blocker is resolved
nodes.detail: timeout after the closure request's validity window

nodes.headline: With that blocker resolved, is anything else in the way?
one blocker cleared, others remain and are surfaced
nodes.detail: each remaining blocker is named and resolved on its own, and closure is requested again - stacking them into one message tells the account holder nothing they can act on

nodes.headline: closure request lapsed with blockers outstanding
nodes.detail: a fresh request re-enters against whatever blockers still stand

nodes.headline: closure not permitted
nodes.detail: the preventing condition changing re-opens this. The account stays open and the reason is on record rather than left as an unexplained refusal

nodes.headline: Execute the account closure. This ends the account relationship and does nothing else - it cancels no subscription unless a contract explicitly couples them, and it deletes no data. The audit and history are untouched
Verify the account is no longer active for the operations closure prohibits
Did the closure take effect?
Account closure → reconcile external and commercial dependencies → finalize
nodes.detail: a closure that has taken effect on the account itself

nodes.headline: Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: a closure that did not fully apply

edges.label: Authorised
edges.when: they own the account or hold the role that may close it

edges.label: Not authorised
edges.when: the request comes from someone who cannot make it

edges.label: Permitted
edges.when: no blocker stands in the way

edges.label: Blocked, recoverable
edges.when: an active financial obligation, an open transaction, a required return, a security review, a dependent entity or an administrative process stands in the way and can be resolved

edges.label: Blocked, not recoverable
edges.when: something prevents closure that the account holder cannot resolve

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the surfaced blocker is resolved

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a closure request held open indefinitely against an unresolved blocker is neither a closure nor a refusal, and the account holder cannot tell which they have

edges.label: All clear
edges.when: no blocker remains

edges.label: Further blockers
edges.when: resolving one revealed or left others

edges.label: Closed
edges.when: the account no longer permits prohibited operations

edges.label: Not fully applied
edges.when: the account remains active somewhere
a closure that has taken effect on the account itself
a closure that did not fully apply

distinctFrom.because: RET-29 completes a subscription cancellation - a commercial relationship ending. An account can be closed with subscriptions running, and a subscription can be cancelled with the account intact.

guardrails: Account closure is not data deletion.
Account closure is not subscription cancellation unless a contract explicitly couples them.
Closure does not silently erase audit or history.
A blocker is named specifically. An unexplained refusal is not a blocker, it is a support case.
governance.reusableRule: Account closure ends an account relationship only after obligations that legitimately block closure have been resolved.
governance.entityScope: the account and this closure request
governance.entityNote: Closing the account ends the account relationship. It cancels no subscription and deletes no data, and neither of those happens as a side effect of it.

identity.categoryTitle: Entity merge, account closure, data lifecycle & terminal states
identity.title: Account closure → reconcile external and commercial dependencies → finalize
identity.purpose: Make sure nothing that lives outside the account is assumed to have ended because the account did.

requires: an account closure that has taken effect on the account itself

nodes.headline: Account closure executing or finalizing

Inventory the external and dependent state: subscriptions, external billing agreements, third-party services, active entitlements, pending invoices, external reservations and linked contracts. Each is a relationship in its own right, and closing an application account has never cancelled a subscription billed by someone else
Does an authoritative contract or system state that this dependency terminates with the account?

Verify the termination actually happened rather than assuming it. A provider reporting success is a statement about their API, and a coupling written into a contract is not the same as a coupling implemented in a system
Record that this dependency requires its own termination and raise it as such. It does not end because our account did, and the person is told which relationships they still hold
until the required dependency outcomes are recorded
nodes.detail: timeout after the closure policy's window for dependency resolution

nodes.headline: Did every required dependency reach its terminal state?
Record each dependency's final state independently of the account's. They are separate relationships and their endings are separate facts, recorded as such

Record which dependencies did not terminate, visibly and by name. A failure to end one dependency is never hidden behind an account marked CLOSED - that is exactly how someone keeps being charged by a provider they believe they have left
Does the closure policy permit the account to close while this dependency remains?
Record the remaining dependency independently, with its own state and its own owner, so it stays visible and attributable after the account is gone
Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: a dependency that did not terminate and cannot be left outstanding

nodes.headline: dependencies reconciled and recorded independently of the account
nodes.detail: a dependency discovered later is reconciled on its own, against the closed account's record

edges.label: Explicitly coupled
edges.when: a contract or the provider's own system says closing the account ends it

edges.label: Independent
edges.when: nothing authoritative couples them - the ordinary case

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the required dependency outcomes are recorded

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a dependency left unresolved is someone continuing to be charged or committed after they believed they had finished, and it does not become resolved by the account looking closed

edges.label: All resolved
edges.when: each dependency reached a recorded end state

edges.label: Some did not
edges.when: at least one dependency failed to terminate

edges.label: Permitted
edges.when: policy allows the account to close with the dependency tracked separately

edges.label: Not permitted
edges.when: the dependency must resolve before closure finalises
a dependency that did not terminate and cannot be left outstanding

guardrails: Closing an application account is never assumed to cancel an externally billed subscription.
An external provider's reported success is verified rather than trusted.
A failure to terminate one dependency is not hidden behind an account marked CLOSED.
Each dependency's final state is recorded independently of the account's.
governance.reusableRule: Account closure and commercial termination are independent state transitions unless an authoritative dependency explicitly couples them.
governance.entityScope: the closing account plus each external or commercial dependency, individually
governance.entityNote: Each dependency is its own relationship with its own end state. None of them ends because our account record changed.

identity.categoryTitle: Entity merge, account closure, data lifecycle & terminal states
identity.title: Closure completed → wind-down → former or terminal account state
identity.purpose: Stop normal account activity while letting the obligations that outlive closure actually finish.

requires: a closure that has been executed and verified

nodes.headline: Account closure succeeded

Suppress new acquisition, normal usage, engagement journeys that are now obsolete, and every account action incompatible with closure - including anything already queued. A closed account receiving an onboarding email is the clearest possible evidence that the closure did not reach everything

Guard against reactivation. A stale login, a queued onboarding step or a delayed synchronisation must not bring a closed account back - closure is a state that later events are checked against, never one they can silently overwrite
Do obligations remain outstanding against this account?
Allow only the scoped processes those obligations need, enumerated individually. A wind-down left as a general exception is an open account with a different label on it
until all outstanding operational obligations complete
nodes.detail: timeout after the wind-down horizon

nodes.headline: Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: a wind-down outliving its horizon

nodes.headline: FORMER; the relationship is over and the historical record is intact
nodes.detail: a returning customer opens a new relationship rather than reviving this one. A terminal relationship state does not mean the records never existed - deleting them is a separate lifecycle with its own request, its own scope and its own authority

edges.label: Obligations remain
edges.when: a final invoice, a refund, a data export, a return, an open support case, a regulatory retention or an external dependency is still outstanding

edges.label: Nothing outstanding
edges.when: the account owes nothing and is owed nothing

edges.label: on event
edges.when: all outstanding operational obligations complete

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: an account held open in wind-down indefinitely is neither closed nor operating, and nobody is left watching which obligation is holding it there
a wind-down outliving its horizon

guardrails: A closed account does not reactivate through a stale login or a queued onboarding event.
The wind-down capability is explicitly scoped and enumerated.
A terminal relationship state does not mean the historical record is deleted.
governance.reusableRule: Closure ends normal account activity while allowing explicitly required wind-down obligations to finish.
governance.entityScope: the closed account and the obligations still outstanding against it
governance.entityNote: The wind-down capability is enumerated rather than left as a general exception, so a closed account cannot quietly keep behaving like an open one.

identity.categoryTitle: Entity merge, account closure, data lifecycle & terminal states
identity.title: Data deletion request → validate scope → hold, delete or retain required data
identity.purpose: Decide what a deletion request actually covers, and keep only what an authoritative retention obligation genuinely requires.

requires: a deletion request naming a data subject and a scope
insufficientAlone: an account closure, which ends a relationship and requests nothing about data
a subscription cancellation
an unsubscribe, which withdraws permission to contact rather than requesting removal

nodes.headline: Data deletion requested
Is the requester's identity and authority established for this scope?
Verification requirement → collect evidence → resume blocked process
nodes.detail: a deletion request whose requester is not yet verified

nodes.headline: Validate the scope, the jurisdiction and policy context, and which systems and data classes are actually in scope. A deletion request is bounded by what it asks for and by what the governing policy covers - not by everything we happen to hold about the person
Inventory the data in scope and classify each item as DELETABLE, RETAIN_REQUIRED, DEPENDENCY_BLOCKED, ALREADY_DELETED or MANUAL_REVIEW
Does an authoritative retention obligation cover any of it?

Retain only what an authoritative obligation actually requires, recording which obligation and why. No retention rule is invented - where policy is silent the data is not kept on a guess, because retaining on a guess keeps what should have gone just as surely as deleting on one destroys what had to stay
What remains, and can it be deleted?
until the blocking dependency clears
nodes.detail: timeout after the request's SLA

nodes.headline: Data deletion execution → propagate → verify or reconcile failure
nodes.detail: data approved for deletion or anonymization

nodes.headline: Decision request → validate → route, reject or hold
nodes.detail: a classification or dependency the automated path could not settle

nodes.headline: nothing in scope to delete; retained items recorded with their obligations
nodes.detail: this is recorded as what it is rather than reported as a deletion. Data arriving later within the same scope is assessed against this request where the policy allows

edges.label: Established
edges.when: the requester is verified as the data subject or as authorised to act for them

edges.label: Not established
edges.when: identity or authority has not been verified to the level this request requires
a deletion request whose requester is not yet verified

edges.label: Retention required
edges.when: a legal or business obligation names data that must be kept

edges.label: Nothing retained
edges.when: no obligation covers anything in scope

edges.label: Deletable and clear
edges.when: data remains in scope, is eligible, and no dependency blocks it

edges.label: Blocked by a dependency
edges.when: something in scope cannot be removed until a dependency clears

edges.label: Needs manual review
edges.when: the classification could not be settled automatically

edges.label: Nothing left
edges.when: everything in scope is already absent or retained under an obligation

edges.label: on event
edges.when: the blocking dependency clears

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: a deletion request usually carries a legal deadline, and a dependency that has not cleared inside it needs a person rather than more waiting
data approved for deletion or anonymization
a classification or dependency the automated path could not settle

distinctFrom.because: Closing an account ends a relationship and requests nothing about data. A deletion request concerns data and says nothing about whether the relationship continues. Either can happen without the other.

guardrails: Account closure is not a deletion request.
A deletion request is not immediate physical deletion of every record.
No retention rule is invented. Where the governing policy is silent, data is not retained on a guess.
Audit evidence may need retaining without retaining the operational data alongside it.
governance.reusableRule: Data deletion removes data according to defined scope while preserving only information that an authoritative retention obligation requires.
governance.entityScope: the data subject, this deletion request, and the data scope it names
governance.entityNote: The request is bounded by what it asks for and by what governing policy covers. It is not a licence to delete everything we hold, nor a reason to keep everything we would rather not lose.

identity.categoryTitle: Entity merge, account closure, data lifecycle & terminal states
identity.title: Data deletion execution → propagate → verify or reconcile failure
identity.purpose: Carry a deletion through every system it has to reach, and keep any part that did not arrive visible.

requires: an approved deletion scope, per system and data class, from a validated request

nodes.headline: Data approved for deletion

Generate the scoped operation for each affected system - delete, anonymize, detach, restrict or place under retention hold - according to what the governing requirement for that system actually is. One operation type applied everywhere either destroys what had to be kept or keeps what had to go

Execute idempotently, keyed so a redelivered job does not repeat an operation, and so that nothing propagates back through downstream synchronisation to recreate what was just removed. A sync job running on its own schedule will otherwise restore a profile deleted an hour earlier, undoing the work while reporting success
until all system confirmations arrive, or a system reports failure
nodes.detail: timeout after the deletion SLA

nodes.headline: How did the operations end?
Was a further copy of the data discovered while the request was running?
Generate and execute the operation for the newly discovered copy, within the same job and the same scope

Record the discovered copy as out of scope, naming why. It is not deleted on this request and it is not left unrecorded either - an unrecorded copy is one nobody knows to assess against the next request

Verify that no required target remains unintentionally active or searchable, to whatever guarantee each system actually offers. The deletion audit records what was removed and when, without keeping a copy of the personal data it removed - an audit that preserves the record has recreated the thing the deletion was for
Did verification confirm every required terminal state?
VERIFIED_COMPLETE; every in-scope obligation reached its terminal state
nodes.detail: a later request covering different scope is its own job. Deletion succeeding in the primary store was never the same as deletion everywhere, and this state records that everywhere was checked

nodes.headline: Record PARTIAL_DELETION_FAILURE, naming which systems did not reach their required terminal state. This is never represented as complete - a deletion reported as done while a downstream copy survives is the most consequential false report in this library, because it ends the investigation that would have found the copy
Is a retry available within the policy budget?
Retry the outstanding operations only, idempotently, so a partially completed deletion is completed rather than restarted
Responsibility escalation → higher authority → resolution or return
nodes.detail: a deletion that could not reach its required terminal state everywhere

edges.label: on event
edges.when: all system confirmations arrive, a system reports failure

edges.label: on timeout
edges.when: silence from a system is not confirmation, and a deletion whose SLA passes with systems unheard from is a partial failure that has not reported itself

edges.label: All confirmed
edges.when: every required system reported its operation complete

edges.label: Some failed
edges.when: at least one system reported failure or did not confirm

edges.label: In scope
edges.when: a copy was found that the approved scope covers

edges.label: Out of scope
edges.when: a copy was found that the approved scope does not cover

edges.label: Nothing further
edges.when: no new copy surfaced

edges.label: Verified
edges.when: every in-scope target reached its required state

edges.label: Something remains
edges.when: a target is still present where it should not be

edges.label: Retry
edges.when: the failure is transient and the budget fixed at the first failure has room

edges.label: Escalate
edges.when: the failure is not clearing, or the budget is spent
a deletion that could not reach its required terminal state everywhere

guardrails: Deletion succeeding in the primary store is not deletion everywhere.
A failed downstream deletion is never represented as fully complete.
Deletion jobs do not recreate profiles through downstream synchronisation.
The deletion audit does not itself preserve the personal data that was deleted.
governance.reusableRule: Distributed deletion is complete only when all in-scope deletion obligations have reached their required terminal state or an explicit retained exception is recorded.
governance.entityScope: the deletion job and each affected system's operation individually
governance.entityNote: Each system's operation has its own type and its own terminal state. A single overall status hides the one that failed, which is the only one that matters.
